evidence.title: Vyra (YC F26) is building the personal video editing agent for shortform content.
evidence.text:
Vyra (YC F26) is building the personal video editing agent for shortform content. 

Today, creators, businesses, and founders are spending hours manually editing content. Vyra learns your taste and edits autonomously, vastly speeding up the pace of content creation and enabling anyone to post consistently.

→ Turn messy recordings into viral videos in minutes
Whether it’s talking head footage, launch videos, or hours of random clips - Vyra consolidates your story and makes it social-ready. 

→ Build personalized video libraries
Directly import reference videos from Instagram or TikTok. Vyra will analyze the style and apply it to your own projects + templatize your own video formats so edits are done in minutes. 

→ Edit from anywhere
With Vyra’s agents running on the cloud, you can upload your footage, give it your prompt, and close the app. Check back in, and the video will be done.

Vyra’s users are already making daily reels for founder-led content, creating 1000s of UGC videos with the MCP, editing personal vlogs, and everything else in between.

Sulan is a creator with over 80k+ followers on Instagram, and Caleb is a video editor of 7 years who previously built plugins for Premiere Pro, Davinci Resolve, and After Effects. As a creator + editor team who both left Brown CS to build Vyra, they experienced this problem firsthand, and now they’re out to solve it.

Create now at usevyra.com or check our link in bio!

Congrats on the launch, Sulan and Caleb!

Vyra (YC F26) is building the personal video editing agent for shortform content. 

Today, creators, businesses, and founders are spending hours manually editing content. Vyra learns your taste and edits autonomously, vastly speeding up the pace of content creation and enabling anyone to post consistently.

→ Turn messy recordings into viral videos in minutes
Whether it’s talking head footage, launch videos, or hours of random clips - Vyra consolidates your story and makes it social-ready. 

→ Build personalized video libraries
Directly import reference videos from Instagram or TikTok. Vyra will analyze the style and apply it to your own projects + templatize your own video formats so edits are done in minutes. 

→ Edit from anywhere
With Vyra’s agents running on the cloud, you can upload your footage, give it your prompt, and close the app. Check back in, and the video will be done.

Vyra’s users are already making daily reels for founder-led content, creating 1000s of UGC videos with the MCP, editing personal vlogs, and everything else in between.

Sulan is a creator with over 80k+ followers on Instagram, and Caleb is a video editor of 7 years who previously built plugins for Premiere Pro, Davinci Resolve, and After Effects. As a creator + editor team who both left Brown CS to build Vyra, they experienced this problem firsthand, and now they’re out to solve it.

Create now at usevyra.com or check our link in bio!

Congrats on the launch, Sulan and Caleb!

evidence.title: Claude Code + Spacesheep: How I Stay in the Loop
evidence.text:
Spacesheep is Claude Code artifacts on steroids: visual, interactive docs, plans and PR reviews, with comments and sharing. It's how I keep up with code that AI writes for me. This is my workflow with Claude Code and Spacesheep, start to finish, on a real feature for Semantic Router v1.

We see what Spacesheep is and what people build with it. Then I plan the feature on a roadmap, have Claude Code (through Spacesheep) write a visual doc of the code I'm about to change, question the options with Spacesheep's built-in agent, and review the result on one page: a decision timeline, the API change, code notes and benchmarks.

How I use Spacesheep:
- Plan first: a roadmap linked to the issues in Linear, then a short plan for the feature.
- Understand: ask for an interactive doc of the code, with the key snippets explained, and say why you want it so the agent can tailor it.
- Discuss: question the agent's suggestions on the page itself, and choose between the options it lays out.
- Review: a PR page with a timeline of every decision (which calls were mine), the code that changed, and what was measured.

🐑 Spacesheep (3 months of pro free): https://spacesheep.dev/join/james?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=creator&utm_campaign=james-briggs&utm_content=ss-1

The feature from this video, now merged and released in semantic-router v1.0.2:
https://github.com/aurelio-labs/semantic-router/pull/778

evidence.title: Introducing: Norn - Artificial intuition for marketing
evidence.text:
AI makes producing content easier. Deciding what’s worth saying is still hard.

We’re Native (YC F26), and we’re building Norn: a model designed to predict which marketing ideas will resonate. It uses brand context, performance, trends and human feedback to rank ideas before content is created.

Norn v1 is already live inside Native, used by more than 2,000 businesses. Native creates and publishes the content, bringing the results back into the learning loop.

In this video, we explain our bet: knowing what to make becomes more valuable as making it gets cheaper.

Next up: the Norn API. 

Join the waitlist: https://native.no/norn

evidence.text:
“Other Side” 
48” x 28”
oil on canvas
2025

this piece was inspired by this semester’s constant debate in my head of whether to chase my dreams or sell out 😭

on the other side of a window lies a brighter promise of greener grass and whimsical frolicking and dream chasing. flowers are blooming…birds are singing…and on days like this, im crashing out about what i should do with my life. which, especially given the recent events at brown, feels like a privilege to think about. how lucky i am to even have the chance to do what i truly want with my life, when life itself is not guaranteed.

here’s to (maybe hopefully probably) chasing my dreams???

We're excited to welcome Matt Strauss to the Ignition Benefits team as our Founding Partnerships Lead.

While most are focused on building pipelines, Matt has spent his career building communities. Through events, content, webinars, and partner programs, he brought SMBs, investors, and clients together around shared goals, and turned those relationships into lasting growth. 

His philosophy is simple: start with the "why" then build partnerships where everyone wins. That's exactly the mindset he's bringing to Ignition as we build a partner ecosystem around a better way to deliver healthcare benefits.

Outside of work, Matt's focused on his favorite partnership yet: raising his 9-month-old daughter with his wife. When he's not building connections at work, he's hunting for the best poke bowl in town — so we're expecting some strong recommendations soon.

Welcome to the team, Matt!

Welcome to the team, Sean.

evidence.title:
Native Autopilot is live 🚀

Before, we said you could put your marketing on autopilot. That was mostly true. You still had to approve or decline every post.

Now you don't even do that.

Native Autopilot is the first fully end-to-end marketing service.

It searches the internet for trends.

It matches them with your business context.

It generates the post, schedules it at your most optimal time, and picks the right platforms.

Then it reads the analytics and learns how to do it better next time.

And it does this for organic and performance content.

Native generates your ads the same way. It automatically spins up new versions of the best performing ones and turns off the ones that aren't working.

It's just a toggle on the Native dashboard.

It's the easiest it has ever been to start creating content for your business.

Fully autonomous. No finger lifting required.

Try it out now with the link in comments 🔥

Today, Index Law (YC F26) is launching Mike-1, an AI legal agent that understands your business, gets legal work done, and brings in exceptional human lawyers when you need them.

Give Mike a contract to negotiate. It reviews the agreement, explains the risks, prepares redlines, and helps get it ready for signature. You review and approve the work along the way.

When a matter needs a human lawyer, Mike brings in a vetted specialist with the documents and context already prepared. Your contracts, past negotiations, and company knowledge stay in one place to inform future work.

Our ambition is to make the capabilities of a great law firm available as software.

We just ran an AI agents workshop at Harvard Business School for the Data Science and AI for Leaders class.

We covered what agents are, how to build them, why they’re useful, and how to actually deploy them. The best part was showing how easily students can spin up and use an OpenClaw agent through Maritime.

A bunch of HBS students walked out with live agents, which is exactly the point. 

The agent wave gets much bigger when deployment stops being the bottleneck.

Excited to do more workshops at MIT and Akamai in the coming days.

Thank you Rem Koning, Sundai, Serge Didenko Vasylechko, and Nash Gadre for leading such a great class

evidence.text:
this is not to say that any path is more meaningful than the other - to be an artist is incredibly admirable and i deeply respect creatives who dedicate their lives to their work

i’ve simply realized that, in these past months, what drew me close to art is the creative process itself which can be translated to other practices. i found the world of entrepreneurship and startups adjacent to the world of painting - you materialize ideas into existence and then let them be held, shaped, and felt by others

how amazing it is to be a creator, regardless of what tools you yield. whether it be a paintbrush, pen, video, or code :)

incredibly grateful to @meeden.art for the lovely studio setup. many hours have already been spent here <3

you can find your own easel and supplies here - https://meedenart.com/?sca_ref=10544193.ZK8AdYhgvo and use code SULANSART at checkout :)

evidence.text:
Everyone in SF loves to give advice.

"You shouldn't post, it's a waste of time"
"You should go viral so that you get more inbound"
"Don't go to events, they don't help"
"Go to events, you will meet cool people that might become your clients"
"Talk to users, they will tell you what you should build"
"Be firm with what you actually want the world to look like because people just haven't caught up"

And so much more...

The right answer?

Yours.

Everyone that ever built something successful made their own opinion, stuck to it and executed on it.

When people see your success, you will create your own advice.

evidence.title:
We’re hosting a hands-on session during Boston TECH WEEK by a16z on something people keep asking for: how to actually deploy an AI agent that works in the real world.

Most people are still stuck at the “prompt in a chatbox” stage. This workshop is about going further. We’ll get you set up with a working agent on the cloud using OpenClaw, ZeroClaw, NemoClaw, or Hermes Agent, and then spend time on what actually matters - configuring it for your specific use case so it’s not just a demo, but something you’d actually use.

We’ll also introduce shareable configs on Maritime. Instead of starting from scratch every time, you’ll be able to take a proven setup, adapt it, and deploy in minutes. And if you build something useful, you can turn it into a template and share it with others - your team, your friends, or anyone who wants to build on top of it.

This is where it gets fun. Instead of one-off agents, you start seeing reusable setups that people tweak, share, and actually use.

If you’ve been curious about AI agents but haven’t had a clean way to try them, this is for you. No tech experience required.

evidence.title: My name is Farqaleet, but most people call me Kiani. I’ve always loved building things.
evidence.text:
My name is Farqaleet, but most people call me Kiani. I’ve always loved building things. 

As a kid I took things apart and found ways to put them back together. So in university i pursued a degree in mechatronics engineering. I’ve worked at AMD, General Motors and was a Senior Software Engineer at Tesla. 

Over the years I had the privilege to mentor many bright young minds. One day my mentee ( Haris ) told me about an idea he had with his friend Vikram, he wanted to build the future of AI Wearables, and he wanted me to help lead the hardware. 

I had originally hired Haris for this drive and energy, and he would always pitch me startup ideas. I was intrigued because I love hardware and found the AI Wearable space very interesting. It was a tough decision, could I really leave a stable job at Tesla to work at a startup? But I thought about it, and if there’s anyone who could disrupt this space, it’s Haris. 

I believed in the vision from that moment on, and I packed my bags and moved to San Francisco to start VEXO. Now we’re gearing up for Demo Day at Y Combinator. 

Follow our journey.

evidence.title:
We were proud to support EmTech 2026 by MIT Technology Review at the MIT Media Lab and help give business leaders direct access to AI agents in the cloud.

A big barrier so far has been simple: many people are interested in agents, but have not had an easy way to actually try them. During the workshop, attendees were able to launch OpenClaw agents fast and securely through Maritime and start interacting with the technology directly.

We think that matters because accessibility is what drives adoption.

What is coming next with Maritime is even more interesting: power users will be able to configure agents for very specific use cases and share those setups with others through shareable configs. 

That means people will not have to start from scratch every time. 

They will be able to build on top of proven agent setups, adapt them to their needs, and help create a growing library of specialized agents.

And increasingly, those agents won’t just live in isolation. They can be registered and discovered through open systems like Project NANDA: The Internet of AI Agents, making them accessible across teams and organizations.

That is where things start to scale.

Anthropic reported that a Houthi cell in northern Yemen used Claude to write the guidance software for a guided rocket and a ballistic missile. They test-fired one. It failed. They went back to Claude to ask why!!
 
Same tools, different weapons. One carries a warhead. The other carries a lie.

Provenance is not a feature. It is, if nothing else, the ethical duty of every company that generates AI content.

Provenance is not a feature. It is, if nothing else, the ethical duty of every company that generates AI content.

The model can recognize the words — but the output still isn’t ready to use.

evidence.title: “longing”
evidence.text:
“longing”
acrylic + oil on canvas
2026

the assignment: ACHOO - how do we experience the “sound” of text in a painting?

i recently came across this song (pickup by @zachdoaa) and i’ve been quite obsessed - smth about the soft and angelic qualities. it inspired much of the colors and qualities of this piece 

more on “longing” - so often i catch myself longing for more, comparing to others who seem to have it figured out. but this comparison game is draining. approaching each day with what i lack leads to misery 

so as i finish my second year of college, im trying to discard this desire and seek gratitude. as i write this, the sun is shining brightly, the temperature is just right. a friend walked by and we exchanged a few words!

if, instead of longing, i simply made peace with what i have - i think that’s what i aspire to achieve

beyond grateful for all of you who listen to my ramblings and give me time of day too :)

may you also find peace and gratitude in the life you have now <3

evidence.title: I always thought that the best day of my life would be the day I resign from my corporate job.
evidence.text:
I always thought that the best day of my life would be the day I resign from my corporate job.
I was wrong.

I’d been working there for a few years.
I was going to resign and focus on my startup idea.

At the office that day, my eyes sought my director.
“Can we talk?” I asked him.
He immediately understood what was about to happen.
“We were going to promote you,” he said as soon as we stepped into a corner.

When he realized that I would not give up on my idea, he made me an offer.
‘’Go on unpaid leave. We’ll keep paying your insurance. Try to do the project you have in mind. If it doesn’t work, come back.’’ he said with a smile on his face.
I realized that he was willing to invest money in the possibility of my project failing, and he did not see a few months of insurance payments as a risk.

I was sweating,
I couldn't decide.
If he could bet on my failure, maybe, in fact, I was going to fail.

This couldn't have been the best day of my life.
I was wrong.

I responded, "I can't leave any open doors behind me." and resigned.
My notice period ended.
And a month later I was free.

I woke up late that first Monday morning.
I prepared a nice breakfast.
I sipped my coffee.
I took a look at my project.
I was free.
I was happy.
I was enthusiastic.

The best day of my life
Wasn’t the day I resigned from my corporate job.
It was the Monday after...

evidence.title:
Lark (YC F26) helped Interline Hardware save 60 hours a month managing inventory and purchasing across 60,000+ items.


Interline Hardware is a wholesale hardware supplier that has served contractors and trade professionals for more than 20 years. 

Their purchasing team went from spending three hours a day assembling a reorder list to about 30 minutes reviewing and approving it.

Across their inventory, Lark (YC F26) helps them:
- Catch missed reorders and identify stockout risks earlier.
- Keep reorder points current, instead of reviewing them only every three to six months.
- Identify excess inventory risks and avoid tying up cash in unnecessary stock.
- Plan purchases around demand, stock on hand, incoming orders, supplier lead times, and seasonality.

Lark (YC F26) connects to their existing ERP and continuously analyzes sales history, stock levels, and open purchase orders. Each purchasing recommendation includes a suggested quantity, cost, and reason for ordering.

The team reviews the recommendations, checks the supporting data, adjusts quantities, and approves purchases.

“It’s also caught items I'd overlooked, and we have more time to get other work done.”
— Mike, Head of Purchasing, Interline Hardware

From kickoff to first use took less than a month. We handled the ERP connection and walked the purchasing team through Lark using Interline’s own items.

Full story at https://lnkd.in/dkUvZD4d

evidence.title:
Huge milestone achieved - We've added a 1:1 model of our proof-of-concept vehicle to one of the most popular " video games 🎮 " BeamNG GmbH.

Now, anyone, anywhere in the world can experience our electric UTVs. ⚡ 🌏  

But adding our proof-of-concept vehicle to BeamNG isn't just a marketing play, we're actually using it to develop our vehicles. 

Calling BeamNG a video game is a disservice - it's actually a real-time soft body physics simulator that takes into account hundreds of vehicle and environmental attributes for a truly realistic driving experience.

To drive our vehicle, you can search "Super Powers Mobility EPEX" in the in-game Mod Repository.

If you don't know about BeamNG, here are some important bragging points.

- BeamNG uses soft-body physics, simulating frame flex, suspension deformation, and real crash behavior.

- Vehicles are built from thousands of nodes and beams, letting you tune springs, dampers, weight, and geometry accurately.

- BeamNG supports fully customizable electric powertrains, including torque curves, regen, thermal limits, and multi-motor setups.

- Off-road surfaces (sand, mud, rock, gravel) have true physical traction models, not scripted effects.

- You can import CAD-derived geometry, enabling early testing of packaging, weight distribution, and chassis layout.

- BeamNG lets you script custom traction control and torque-vectoring logic through LUA.

- BeamNG is used by OEMs, researchers, and universities via BeamNG.tech for real engineering simulation.

- Built-in sensors (IMU, wheel speed, GPS, LiDAR) allow telemetry-accurate testing.

- You can run durability tests—rollovers, jumps, impacts—previously impossible to do without burning tons of capital on simulation or real-world parts.

#BeamNG #Simulation #ElectricOffroad #EVUTV #SuperPowersMobility

evidence.text:
Everyone says software has no moat anymore. I’m building a software company anyway.

An agent writes most of our code. And I have more conviction in Roma than in anything I’ve built before. Here’s why 🧵

Almost every early Roma user tells us they tried to build it themselves first.

Hook a to-do app up to Claude, add a few scripts, connect the inbox. It works once. Then it falls apart.

We know. We tried it too.

The hardest part is the interface.

What happens when you say three things in one breath? Where does the result show up so you actually see it? How do you steer the agent when it’s wrong?

Everyone underestimates good UX, even now.

Then there’s the harness: getting the agent to do the same thing the same way every time.

When we simplified Roma’s interface mid-batch, the AI got more reliable too. Same problem.

AI made the first 80% easier. The last 20% is where the moat lives.

You make the agent, the skills, and the prompts. We run the sandboxes and keep the files and the memory of each agent. When you get more customers, we add more sandboxes.

Thus, you can select a different harness each week, and your customers always get the best agent.

Try Agent37 today.

evidence.title:
Today, Caveman becomes a company.

It started as a simple idea that got 88k GitHub stars: AI systems should stop wasting tokens.

Now we are building the infrastructure behind it.

Caveman is developing a new efficiency layer for AI: models, gateways, and tools that reduce unnecessary reasoning, compress verbose outputs, and make agentic systems faster and cheaper without sacrificing performance.

The goal is not to make AI say less for the sake of brevity.
The goal is to remove waste from every layer of the stack.

That means:
• more efficient models
• compressed reasoning and outputs
• lower inference costs
• faster agent workflows
• measurable savings for teams running AI at scale

The next generation of AI will not only be more capable.
It will be radically more efficient.
This is day one.

evidence.title:
Ascenix is joining Y Combinator's Fall 2026 batch!

Ascenix started with a simple mission: Help senior care teams use the data they already collect to improve resident outcomes.

Rishi and Ayaan spent over a year living in a retirement home, working alongside residents and care teams to understand the problems they face every day. The learnings from that experience have grown into a platform supporting 50+ senior care facilities.

Today, Ascenix is building the incident intelligence layer for long-term care: turning everyday clinical documentation into automated reporting, compliance insights, and a clearer picture of resident risk.

Joining YC is an exciting next chapter for us as we continue building Ascenix and we’re incredibly grateful to our team, customers, advisors, investors, and everyone who has believed in us along the way. We’re just getting started 🚀.

evidence.title:
Last week, we officially launched Trepo (YC F26) with Y Combinator.

Here are the two products we released:

1. Trepo Kitchen Assistant
Our production-grade kitchen assistant, designed to live in your kitchen. It helps households keep track of what they have, figure out what to cook, reduce food waste, and take the mental load out of managing food at home (preorder today!).

2. Trepo Shopping Agent
An entirely new way to shop for groceries. Instead of manually building lists, comparing prices, and placing orders, Trepo understands what your household has, uses, and needs, then shops on your behalf.

What excites me most is what happens when these two products work together.

Finish a carton of milk? Hold it under the Kitchen Assistant. In the background, Trepo finds the best deal, buys it, and adds it to your next delivery.

No lists. No remembering. No unnecessary trips to the store.

We believe buying groceries should be effortless, and knowing what to buy shouldn't be your responsibility.

Couldn't be more stoked to be building this.

Preorders are now open. See link in the comments below 🚀

evidence.title:
Last week was a big milestone for the Aikido team as we officially kicked off A1DC — what we believe will be the world's first floating wind-powered datacenter.

This project will take us from the swampy, humid bayou of Louisiana to the frigid fjords of Norway. And last week our team members were in both locations. 

In Louisiana, retrofit activities began on the A1 platform with our fabrication partner MORRISON Energy. Our fearless CEO Sam Kanner, who may get a bit too involved, and our tireless Lead Engineer Jonathan Nash were on site assisting. One lesson learned already: designing for rapid assembly also makes for impressively fast disassembly.

Meanwhile our Norwegian team members were in Haugesund, Norway sharing the details of our project at Floating Wind Days, with our local partners Norwegian Offshore Wind.  

A1DC is an important step toward demonstrating how offshore wind and AI infrastructure can be deployed together in a new way.
We'll be sharing more details on the project soon. Stay tuned.

evidence.title:
Hesper AI is at the IASIU (International Association of Special Investigation Units) Annual Conference this week. Rosen Shingle Creek, Orlando, September 20 to 23.

Fraudsters got generative AI two years ago. Most SIUs got a bigger caseload and the same number of hours in the day.

That gap is the work. 20+ function-specific agents read every document in a claim, verify the providers and the policy behind it, and check the loss against what actually happened that day. Every finding arrives with its evidence attached, because a finding an SIU cannot defend is not worth having.

The point is not fewer investigators. It is investigators who are faster and much harder to fool. The agents build the case. The person still decides.

We are not here to tell this room how to investigate a claim. Most of the people at this conference were doing it before any of it was software. We are here to make sure the next fabricated invoice does not get past them.

Our CEO, Pankaj Dhariwal, is here through Wednesday. Come find us.

gethesperai.com

evidence.title:
The first generation of legal AI was built for lawyers.

We believe the next generation should be built for the people with the most at stake.

Index Law is introducing Index Intelligence: our research and engineering programme to build frontier legal agents that can understand complete legal matters, not simply answer isolated legal questions.

Its first public release is Assess, available now.

Users explain what happened in their own words and upload their documents. Assess asks the questions that matter, examines the record and builds a structured view of the facts, evidence, risks, unresolved issues, available options and practical next steps.

This is not simply a faster way to navigate the law.

It is a new starting point for legal services, built from the client backwards.

Before spending thousands on legal advice, individuals and businesses should be able to understand the shape of their position, what is at risk and what they can do next.

Behind Assess, we are building our own agent infrastructure, matter-level reasoning systems, evaluations and benchmarks. Our aim is to develop systems that can understand the full context of a legal matter, distinguish evidence from assertion, explain uncertainty and recognize when qualified legal judgment is required.

Assess is the first step towards a broader vision: an AI-native legal institution that makes high quality legal intelligence dramatically more accessible.

The law will always be complicated.

Understanding where you stand should not be.

Read more and try Assess at https://indexlaw.com/

Before you hire a lawyer, Index it.

Most people are curious about AI agents, but still haven’t had a clear way to actually try them.

This Thursday, we’re hosting a hands-on online workshop for business professionals, operators, and founders who want to understand what agents can realistically do.

The session is practical: we’ll set up and configure four OpenClaw agents for common workflows like research, automation, communication, and decision support.

No coding required. No local setup. We’ll run everything in the cloud through Maritime.

The goal is not to hype agents, but to help people see what they are, where they are useful, and how to start using them in real work.

By the end, participants should have their own agents running and a better understanding of how to configure instructions, tools, memory, and access.

If you’ve been hearing a lot about agents and want a more concrete, hands-on starting point, join us this Thursday.

evidence.title:
We just gave agents Android phones.

Developers can now run an agent on its own virtual Android device. It can download apps, navigate them, and use the phone just like a person would.

And if you’re building agents at scale, you can give every agent its own phone so it can access the apps and mobile workflows it needs to do its job.

This opens up an entirely new category of agent capabilities.

Many of the tools people rely on every day are mobile-first. They don’t have an API or an existing agent integration. Until now, that meant agents couldn’t use them.

Now, if a person can do something on an Android phone, an agent can do it too.

evidence.title:
We took a song, compressed it 1,000× with a neural codec, printed it on paper as eight QR codes, scanned it back, and rebuilt the audio.

audio → neural codec → tokens → paper → tokens → neural codec → audio

The DeepMark watermark was still in it.

For a moment the song wasn't audio at all. When it came back, its provenance came back with it. That's the whole idea behind content-bound provenance: the proof lives in the sound, not in the file.

Full write-up, with the audio and the numbers:

https://lnkd.in/dEEhfz2A

evidence.title:
AI search should just feel like finding the answer.

But today, giving an agent access to your docs means building a pipeline first: chunking, embeddings, a vector DB, re-indexing every time something changes. Then you pay to keep it all running, even when no one’s asking.

We built WonderSearch (YC F26) so you can skip all of that.
→ Your agents search your docs semantically, directly. No embeddings, no vector DB, nothing to build or maintain.
→ Plug in any agent via MCP, API, CLI or SDK.
→ $0 when idle (fully serverless)
→ SOTA Sparse Retrieval, beats most dense embedding models (but we require no embeddings)

Drop in your PDFs and docs, and your agents start finding answers.

evidence.title: my favorite method of procrastinating paintings: building canvases 😭
evidence.text:
my favorite method of procrastinating paintings: building canvases 😭

materials:
- wood planks (1x4)
- quarter rounding (for the raised edges of a stretcher)
- brad nailer 
- miter saw
- wood glue 

first, attach quarter rounding (facing inward!) to an edge of the wood planks with wood glue. secure using brad nailer (1-1/4” long nails) - the nails act as temporary binding while the wood glue dries!

then, saw the wood into the dimensions of the stretcher you want. you need to saw off at 45 degrees so that when you put all four perimeter pieces together, they make a rectangle. basically, you should have four trapezoid pieces in the end (2 length pieces and 2 width pieces)

finally, you can attach everything together using wood glue and the brad nailer again (5/8” nails this time) to assemble the corners. and after that you stretch the actual canvas fabric (starting with the center of each side and stapling outwards gradually) and gesso it three times and you’re good to paint :)

#artist #painting #artschool #canvas #stretcher

evidence.title:
One of the most requested features on maritime is now out: residential IPs for your agents.

Most of the web was built for people at home, not servers in a data center. 

Plenty of sites block cloud addresses, show them different results, or log them out. That’s a wall for agents that need to do real work on real websites.

Now an agent on Maritime can go online from a home connection in the country, state or city you pick. To the website, it looks like an ordinary visitor.

What teams use it for:

- Getting into portals and booking sites that refuse cloud traffic
- Checking prices, availability and search results the way a local customer sees them
- Staying logged in: keep the same IP for an agent for up to 24 hours, or get a new one for every connection
- Testing your own product from another country before you launch there

Check it out, now on any plan: https://lnkd.in/gS2T6vpn

evidence.title:
The line between real and synthetic audio is disappearing.

Not in the future. Now.

Our latest analysis of speaker signatures in ElevenLabs voices points in the same direction we keep coming back to:

real = synthetic is inevitable.

Synthetic voices are becoming natural enough that, in many cases, the practical question will no longer be “can humans tell the difference?”
It will be:

How do we verify origin, authenticity, and integrity when the difference no longer matters perceptually?

That shift changes everything.

The world won’t be secured by trying to guess what is fake.
It will be secured by building systems that make authenticity verifiable.

That is why provenance and watermarking matter.

New blog post: https://lnkd.in/ditP4g3q

Our latest analysis of speaker signatures in ElevenLabs voices points in the same direction we keep coming back to:

real = synthetic is inevitable.

Synthetic voices are becoming natural enough that, in many cases, the practical question will no longer be “can humans tell the difference?”
It will be:

How do we verify origin, authenticity, and integrity when the difference no longer matters perceptually?

That shift changes everything.

The world won’t be secured by trying to guess what is fake.
It will be secured by building systems that make authenticity verifiable.

That is why provenance and watermarking matter.

New blog post: https://lnkd.in/ditP4g3q

evidence.text:
One of the best things about AI for a non-technical person like me is it makes it so easy to stay organized. 

This week I was getting frustrated keeping up with all of our outbound efforts (email, ads, linkedin outreach, etc)...Always constantly changing between different tools, trying to see what works and what doesn't. 

So with Claude Code I created a Sales & Growth "Command Center" where we can see revenue, where it's coming from, how all of our outbound campaigns are performing — and it updates every 30 minutes. 

One HTML link that our leadership team can look at anytime they want to see how we're performing, where there are gaps, and what we can do to fix it.

evidence.title:
Phaser Studio Inc. is on a mission to make it easy for anyone to build games.

The new Phaser Game Agent turns a simple user description into a fully functional game, built in real time, fully customized for the user. 

Behind the scenes, the Phaser agent runs in a Superserve sandbox with full access to Phaser's game studio. The game's design, code, art, and sound is crafted by the agent in real-time, and published from within the sandbox.

The user gets back a link to the game, ready to play and to share with their community.

"I wanted a simple API that spins up sandboxes fast, that we could configure, that we could build our own templates on. That's exactly what we got."
— Richard Davey (Founder and CTO, Phaser Studio)

Read the full case study: https://lnkd.in/gGvhRxhy

evidence.title: something I’ve noticed: when a new model comes out, it feels incredible, and everyone is awestruck. but over time, it starts to feel less capable, or maybe it just feels that way b
evidence.text:
something I’ve noticed: when a new model comes out, it feels incredible, and everyone is awestruck. but over time, it starts to feel less capable, or maybe it just feels that way because our expectations keep rising.

when Astra launched, I gave it a reference and asked it to design a CAD model from it. the result was so good that I genuinely wondered whether we even needed in-house industrial designers. yesterday I was working on something and, after dozens of iterations, still couldn’t get what I wanted.

I’ve seen the same thing happen with Claude.

maybe I’m just expecting too much from these models?

Healthcare is one of the largest expenses on the P&L for most employers. Yet many finance leaders still lack the visibility to manage it effectively.

Our latest survey with CFO Leadership puts numbers behind the problem:

• 78% of CFOs say healthcare costs are rising faster than revenue.
• Half say they're rising much faster.
• Only 39% have a clear picture of how their costs compare to similar companies.
• 20% have no access to benchmarking data at all.

When you can't see what's driving your healthcare spend, it's hard to know whether you're overpaying or simply accepting another increase. That's the challenge this research explores, and why better data is the first step toward better decisions.

If your next renewal is on the horizon, these findings are worth your attention:

https://lnkd.in/eBnWPv4e

evidence.title:
I got rejected by Y Combinator three times. On the fourth attempt, we got in.


Here’s what changed:

1. We stopped obsessing over getting into YC.

   VEXO was getting built either way. A yes would make us faster. A no wouldn’t stop us.
2. We built the ugly version.

   With a resin printer in a garage, we made real devices and put them in people’s hands. Build it. Get feedback. Show what changed.

3. We had the team to pull it off.
   Between the three of us, we’d worked at Tesla and Amazon. We trusted each other to turn a prototype into a real product.


My advice: 
make your application a progress update. Give them a company they want in on.


Follow along as we build VEXO.

evidence.title:
A classroom of thirty can't interrogate the teacher. It's no different in law. 

A client can't interrogate their lawyer either.

You absorb the advice, go home, and do the homework. 

The one thing you can't really do is keep asking.

Alan Greenberg's argument: AI is better than a traditional lawyer at the interrogation part, the bit where you finally get to ask. And it's useless at the doing. Once you have the diagnosis, you need someone qualified to turn it into something real.

evidence.title:
RayAI CLI is the fastest way to build agents with parallel tool calling and code execution.

Better agents explore more, but sequential tool calls make exploration slow. Batching them has meant real infra work: task queues, workers, result collection. RayAI handles all of that.

BatchTool lets your agent batch any tool call. The LLM decides when to parallelize, Ray handles the distributed execution. One call, parallel results.

When your agent writes code, it runs in a gVisor sandbox isolated from your infrastructure.

Framework-agnostic. Build with LangChain, Pydantic, or pure Python. Mix tools from different frameworks in the same agent.

Docs: docs.rayai.com
GitHub: https://lnkd.in/ghJEFPKf

evidence.title:
Claude Code can’t see what Codex just wrote.

If you run more than one AI agent, you’ve hit this. Every agent works on its own copy of your files: your laptop has one, Claude Code has one, Codex has another. None of them see each other’s changes, so you end up copying files between them, re-explaining context and working out which version is real.

Today we’re launching WonderDrive by Wondersearch (YC F26): one drive for you and every agent.
→ Codex saves a file, and Claude Code sees it the same second
→ Hand work between you, Claude Code, Codex and Cursor without copying anything
→ Semantic retrieval built in, so agents can find anything on the drive
→ Run and deploy straight from the drive
→ Rewind any change when an agent breaks something

We built it because our own agents kept tripping over each other. Now they share one desk.

WonderDrive is coming soon to every Wondersearch (YC F26) user. 

Sign up for early access: wondersearch.com

Dalton Prescott Ng / Y Combinator / Founders, Inc.

evidence.text:
I’ve noticed a shift in how I work over the past few months.

I used to prefer doing things in the UI. Now I almost avoid it. I’d much rather handle email, calendar, finances, pretty much anything, through MCPs or plugins in 
@Claude
 Code or 
@ChatGPT
.

It’s reached the point where I get annoyed when a tool doesn’t have an integration. Something I wouldn’t even have thought to look for a few months ago is now part of how I decide whether I want to use it.

For everything else, I’ve been using computer use with Astra in Codex, which works really well. But if there’s a plugin, I’m still choosing that first.

evidence.title: big fan of the crunchy paper asmr 🙂‍↕️🙂‍↕️
evidence.text:
big fan of the crunchy paper asmr 🙂‍↕️🙂‍↕️

assignment: “an unreadable script,” a series of 10 ink paintings meant to explore the markmaking related to language, lettering, and typography, while not writing legibly 

realized through this exercise that i love the intimacy of journaling and that quick, speedy scribble which captures fleeting ideas and emotions. a lot of the scribbly text in these paintings were merely my convoluted thoughts as i was working! 

some other strokes that i really love include the markmaking of traditional chinese characters, especially in calligraphy and ink portrayals. each character is a deliberate, delicate effort, and im so sad that i never tried harder to learn how to write chinese (i was always too lazy alas 🥲)

anyway, glad this assignment brought me out of my comfort zone and allowed me to experiment. lowk the quantity over quality emphasis is super helpful to iterate and learn 🤩 when in doubt make 10 iterations of something :>

okay now onto the next!

evidence.title: “Pretty and Peaceful”
evidence.text:
“Pretty and Peaceful”
12 in. x 36 in.
oil on canvas
2025

to me, this piece represents freedom from abusive relationships. though she is mortally wounded, the flowers blossoming from her head symbolize peace upon escaping from what was a drawn-out war. bolder edges and a more vibrant underpainting differentiate this piece from “Bruises and Blooms,” through a greater sense of triumph rather than surrender.

evidence.title: Girişimcilik, kendi kendinin patronu olmak değildir. Müşterileriniz, sizin patronunuzdur.
evidence.text:
Girişimcilik, kendi kendinin patronu olmak değildir. Müşterileriniz, sizin patronunuzdur.

Girişimcilik, havalı, keyifli bir iş değildir.
Acılarla, hayal kırıklıklarıyla doludur.

Ama inanın bana...
Hepimiz çok güçlüyüz.
Çok fazla acıya, zorluğa katlanabiliriz.
Çoğu zaman verdiğimiz savaş dünyayla değil,
Kendi zihnimizle.

Eğer girişimciliğin gerçek yüzünü görmek, detaylarını öğrenmek, her inişin nasıl bir çıkışla sonlanabileceğini görmek isterseniz...

2021 yılının en iyi girişimcilik kitabı seçilen, '5 Parasız Silikon Vadisi' kitabıma göz atabilirsiniz. Linki yorumlara bırakıyorum. :) 

Ve sayın Dr. Bertan Kaya, çok teşekkür ediyorum bu güzel paylaşımınız için!

Do you start over? Which tool calls finished? Did that last write actually happen?

We learned this the hard way building
evidence.text:
Your agent is halfway through a job when the server dies.

Do you start over? Which tool calls finished? Did that last write actually happen?

We learned this the hard way building agents at Parcha and Grep. Our early agents could work for several minutes, hit one provider error near the end and lose their progress. A great demo didn't mean we had a system customers could depend on.

We tried putting more of the work into deterministic pipelines. Recovery got easier, but every new task meant more orchestration code. We wanted agents to have room to reason without making them responsible for remembering everything that happened before a crash.

That's one of the reasons we built AgentRun.

The execution state lives outside the tool sandbox. Runs and their step journals are persisted in SQLite or Postgres, rather than existing only in the process running the agent.

Runners claim work with renewable leases. If a runner dies, another can pick up the run after its lease expires. Recovery uses the recorded results of completed steps instead of executing them again.

The tricky part is a tool call that was in flight when the process died. Retrying a read is different from repeating a write that may already have happened. AgentRun distinguishes safe-to-retry calls from interrupted calls whose outcome needs checking. It doesn't blindly replay everything.

AgentRun also manages the sandbox lifecycle, with support for Docker, Daytona, Modal and more providers coming soon!

This was a big lesson from three years of building agents: the model should be figuring out the work. The system around it should keep track of what happened and make recovery possible. 

You shouldn't have to rebuild that for every agent.

evidence.title: A courtroom transcript needs to capture not just what was said, but who said it. Courtrooms are among the hardest settings for speaker diarization: long hearings, many speakers, fr
evidence.text:
A courtroom transcript needs to capture not just what was said, but who said it. Courtrooms are among the hardest settings for speaker diarization: long hearings, many speakers, frequent interruptions, and overlapping speech.

While working on it, we ran into a limitation of streaming diarization models: they have a fixed number of speaker slots, which get reused when more speakers join the conversation.

Our team at 
@Adalat_AI
  built a training-free linker that lets these models track speakers beyond their slot limit, without retraining. 

On courtroom hearings with up to 23 speakers, cpWER dropped from 82.7% to 24.4%.

Feel free to take a look at the work, I'm sure a lot of folks will find it relevant. 

If you're interested in solving hard speech ML problems with us, please reach out!

evidence.title:
Happy new year to my designer friends!

Hot take: the separation of UX research, UX design, and product design only makes sense when you're building for well-understood users. When
evidence.text:
Happy new year to my designer friends!

Hot take: the separation of UX research, UX design, and product design only makes sense when you're building for well-understood users. When there are existing patterns to reference, best practices to follow, competitors to study.

But what happens when none of that exists?

At 
@Adalat_AI
 , we're building for India's judiciary courtrooms, judges, lawyers, citizens navigating the legal system. No one has studied these workflows. No one has defined these UX patterns. There's no playbook.

In this world, the traditional SaaS model breaks down. You can't have a PM write a spec from research that doesn't exist. You can't have a researcher hand off insights for a designer to "execute." The whole thing has to happen together, in the same head, in the same team.

That's why we don't have traditional PMs. Designers and engineers own the product talking to users, defining problems, shipping. Research and design aren't separate functions, they're intertwined because they have to be.

For the right designer, this is the most exciting kind of problem. You're defining what good looks like for an audience that's never been served.

We're hiring two designers, one to scale a product already in 20% of India's courtrooms, one to build 0→1 with me. Remote-first, India.

Post more, but only with something that actually sounds like you.

evidence.title:
Most legal documents have been written millions of times before. Why are we still paying hourly rates?

Our thesis at Index is that a human lawyer is only needed for the last 20-30% of a case. Not the first 80.

The traditional model bills you for both at the same rate, on the same invoice.
The judiciary's own guideline rate for a Grade A London solicitor is £579 an hour, effective January this year.

The price is defensible for judgment, but it is not a defensible price for research, document assembly, or a contract that has been written millions of times before.

So we charge fixed fees. AI does the repeatable work. A senior lawyer does the last 20%.

Our CEO Quddus on the thesis:

We’re excited to announce that The Rt Hon. Dominic Raab has joined Index Law as Founding Senior Advisor.

Dominic previously served as the UK’s Deputy Prime Minister, Justice Secretary and Foreign Secretary, and practised as an international lawyer before entering government.

He joins Index at an important stage in our development as we build a new model for legal services around AI: software doing more of the work, exceptional lawyers stepping in where judgment matters, and businesses getting legal help faster and more efficiently than the traditional model allows.

As Founding Senior Advisor, Dominic will work closely with the team on strategy, international expansion and the institutional trust required to scale AI-native legal services globally.

We believe the next generation of legal companies won’t simply sell AI to law firms. They’ll rethink how legal work is delivered from the ground up.

We’re very pleased to have Dominic helping us build that future.

Welcome to Index, Dominic.

evidence.text:
I use Claude, Codex and Muse all the time. But using more than one agent means I spend a lot of time moving work between them.

One has the context. Another has the instructions. And I'm trying to remember which chat has the thing I need next.

So I copy, paste and explain it again. Then I go back to find something I forgot to bring over.

The agents are doing the work. I'm chasing it.

I don't want to stop using any of them. I just want to stop being the person holding all the pieces together.

evidence.text:
Seven years ago, we were the centenary batch at 
@IITBHU_Varanasi
. This weekend in Chicago, that journey came full circle.

I got to spend time with fellow IIT BHU alumni. Founders, operators, and builders spanning generations of the same campus that shaped us. Everyone was so approachable that it felt like speaking to college seniors - not CEOs running billion-dollar companies.

Sitting in that room, still early in our journey of building 
@antimattr_one
, I was reminded that how much of path there is ahead and how many people who've walked further are still willing to reach back and pull the next person forward. That's the part of an IIT education no syllabus captures. The classrooms teach you how to think. The network reminds you that you never really build alone.
 
Grateful for the roots. Varanasi to Chicago and beyond. ❤️

Har Har Mahadev

evidence.title: I Need YOUR Help!
evidence.text:
I Need YOUR Help!

Last week I asked my email subscribers to fill out a small questionnaire.
My email open rates skyrocketed,
Higher than it has ever been in a long time.

The subject of that email was: I Need YOUR Help!
And I did need their help.
I genuinely wanted to know what they needed from me
To be able to create better content for them.

When I first started being an affiliate for Cambly,
I was doing a lot of 1:1 reach-outs
My goal was to get them to try Cambly
Then convert to customers of Cambly.
It didn’t work out that well.

What I should have been doing all along was,
Instead of SELLING.
Trying to understand what their NEEDS were.
Once I switched to that
It DID work out much better.

So to celebrate LinkedIn for Creators's suggested #GetToKnowYourCustomersDay
(In my case #GeToKnowYourAudienceDay)
I would love to hear what YOU need from me.

What kind of content helps you more?
Do you prefer written or video content?
What are some topics you would like me to cover?

#content #creator

evidence.title:
DeepSeek's open-source agent harness now runs on Maritime.

dsh came out in August, MIT licensed. The interesting part is the architecture: models, tools, skills, sessions, sandboxes and even the web workbench are all plugins, and every run is written to an append-only session log you can resume, fork and replay.

Running it yourself means keeping a machine up, and the upstream workbench ships without authentication. So we made it a template. One command, or one click from Templates, and you get dsh on its own machine with the workbench behind a per-agent token.

Docs: https://lnkd.in/ea_4UgBU

evidence.title:
imo the bigger issue is 2nd order effects of economic value not being structured around people

part of what incentivizes countries to invest in their people is human capital: bett
evidence.text:
imo the bigger issue is 2nd order effects of economic value not being structured around people

part of what incentivizes countries to invest in their people is human capital: better schools, nutrition, public health, etc improve productive capacity (to be reductive) 

if AI does ~most productive work, that link is broken, and you see this play out in countries dependent on natural resources. the economy, and most investment,  centers around oil/mining and not infrastructure that benefits most people

of course there are many other incentives at play that help with this alignment (e.g. democratic voting, social externalities) but this seems like a pretty fundamental part of the modern social contract

evidence.text:
Webster's Dictionary made "Slop" their word of the year in 2025.

It's not hard to see why.

From poorly "personalized" emails, to em-dashes, to article headlines overusing "delve" "harness" and "unlock"...it's hard for Marketers to cut through the noise.

One thing that helps — research-backed content. 

And one thing AI is actually good at? Running research.

The design partners that have trusted us over this past year have found use-cases for BeHeard we couldn't have dreamed of when we started:

- Thought Leadership Reports
- Message/Position/Concept Testing
- Brand Health Trackers
- Competitive Research
...the list goes on and on

We're excited to help Marketers get actual value from an AI solution, but more importantly we're privileged to learn from some of the best, forward-thinking Marketers in the business.

Since announcing that The Rt Hon. Dominic Raab had joined Index Law as Founding Senior Advisor, the question we've been asked most is what he's actually doing with us. Here is one answer.

Dominic practised as an international lawyer before entering government, and as Lord Chancellor and Justice Secretary was responsible for the Ministry of Justice, the courts and the legal aid system in England and Wales. 

He has also been on the other side of it. After leaving politics he set up a consultancy, found advisers, explained the same situation repeatedly, and still wondered whether everything had been done properly.

If you have legal work you think should be dramatically faster/easier/cheaper and want to work together, email q@indexlaw.com.

evidence.title:
Last month, the SPM team headed into the Nevada desert to put our electric off-road platforms directly in the hands of Special Operations Forces (SOF) technology evaluators. 

We demonstrated the Energized Vehicle Kit (EVK) which can transform any light off-road vehicle into a silent yet high performance vehicle, or it can be added to augment an existing ICE vehicle and add power storage and export capability. 

Over the course of the event, we conducted nearly 100 vehicle demonstrations and logged more than 60 hard miles across high desert terrain on both prototype vehicles. Dust, rain, cold, heat, huge rocks, continuous driver changes, charging in the field, and nonstop operational use in exactly the type of environment these systems are being designed for.

What stood out most wasn’t just the vehicles' endurance. It was the reaction from the operators. Some were blown away by how capable and simple the vehicles were to operate. With others, conversations quickly evolved beyond “electric vehicles” and into operational capability enabled by mobile, energy dense batteries. 

Demonstrations like this are a reminder that SPM's tech is not just a concept, it’s becoming a platform that people want to use in the real world.

#electricUTV #energy #startup #defensetech

evidence.text:
Day 400 of building 
http://
agent37.com

I feel like a fraud saying this out loud...

But here's my actual vision:

A substantial percentage of the world economy could run on Agent37.

Yes, that sounds insane.

But when I think about it:

Models will get smarter.
They'll need orchestration.
They'll need servers.
They'll need to connect to everything.
LLM’s will become local.

And already the more I talk to customers and the more I see how they’re using it, I can see real work being done, real value being created and real economic output all happening in this servers as computations.

If we build the simplest, cheapest, highest-quality layer for that. Maybe we have a shot ?

We will probably need to get lucky a hundred times, maybe more..

But it’s clear that this is the future. Someone’s going to build it, in-fact many will. This is not a winner take all market. And that’s a good thing..

This is just the beginning.

evidence.text:
Up to 60% of the sources AI platforms cite change month to month, per recent search visibility data.

That number should worry anyone who signed off on a content budget expecting the ranking to hold. A citation you earned in March doesn't mean anything to the AI answer in April.

This is turning into a defensibility problem, not just a visibility one. When leadership asks why organic pipeline dipped, "we were cited last quarter" isn't an answer that survives a budget conversation.

The fix isn't publishing more. It's publishing on a cadence that matches how often the actual ranking resets.

evidence.title:
SpaceX raised $75 billion for their IPO earlier this year, but what about the IPOs' legal fees?

They disclosed about $25 million. 

That is one of the highest amount spent on IPO legal fees ever. But it was only 0.034% of their raise.

Arm had to spend $17 million in IPO legal fees, with a $4.8705bn base offering. That's 0.365% of their raise, more than 10x more expensive relative to SpaceX.

Similarly, Robinhood's $2.090bn IPO offering in 2021 cost them $10.030m is legal fees. Almost 0.5% of their raise and more than 14x more expensive relative to SpaceX.

So arguably, SpaceX had one of, if not, the most efficient IPO of all time.

Want to see the full list of the biggest IPOs by legal fees? We broke it down in our first edition of The Ledger, link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
This Thursday, we had the chance to run a five-hour workshop and teach over 500 people how to deploy real AI agents 

At Imagination in Action, we gave all the participants their own OpenClaw agent hosted on Maritime. To be honest, we are a little overwhelmed by the response, but in the best way. People are using it, sharing it, and pushing the product much faster than we expected.

One of the best parts was seeing how quickly people could actually get started. Being able to spin up an agent in about a minute changes the experience completely. No long setup, no painful hosting process, just a fast path from curiosity to a working agent.

We also saw strong response to how simple integrations already are. Telegram was especially easy for people to connect, and we have more integrations and features on the way.

Right now, we are definitely stretching our beta more than planned, but that is because demand has been real. We have more updates coming soon, new features in the works, and a lot of new opportunities ahead.

Very grateful to everyone building with us.

Maria Gorskikh Aryaman Shrivastava Nikolay Vyahhi, Gabriela Torres V., Serge Didenko Vasylechko, Brandon S., Fridolin Haugg, Liliia Botueva Rıza Egehan Asad John Werner

Their entire business is built around
evidence.text:
I think manufacturing software companies are financially incentivized to preserve the very complexity autonomous factories need to eliminate.

Their entire business is built around helping humans manage factories. Scheduling production, tracking orders, managing quality, and coordinating people. The more complicated the factory, the more software you need to manage it.

It's easy to look at a factory and see a bunch of inefficiencies that software should be able to solve.

Then you actually run the floor.

A tool breaks. A part moves during machining. The material arrives late. A setup that worked yesterday doesn't work today. Suddenly, the problem looks very different from what you saw on a dashboard.

When something goes wrong, an experienced operator figures it out. Most of that knowledge never makes it back into the system.

You can't just put AI on top of that and expect the factory to run itself.

If we want truly autonomous factories, the machines, software, inspection, and the way they learn from each other need to be designed together from day one.

The factory itself has to be the product, not just the software running it.

evidence.title: A Robot for Your Parents. Meet Rhem.
evidence.text:
This robot isn't for you... it's for your parents.

Rhem is a health assistant robot for older adults and their families. It helps aging parents stay independent at home while helping their children stay informed about their health, routines, and daily life.

Preorder the Rhem Founding Edition →

Your parents want to do things for themselves. You want to know they’re doing okay. Rhem helps with both.

What can Rhem help your parents with?

Rhem is a voice-first home robot that can help with everyday tasks like:

• Booking appointments
• Ordering groceries
• Making phone calls
• Managing reminders
• Staying on top of daily routines

There are no complicated apps to learn. Your parents can simply talk to Rhem.

Rhem can also help families stay informed about their parents’ health and daily life, making it easier to stay connected even when they can’t be there in person.

Who is Rhem for?
Rhem is designed for older adults who want to maintain their independence at home—and for the sons, daughters, and family members who want peace of mind without taking away that independence.

Who is behind Rhem?

We’re Jacob and Huey, the father–son founders of Rhem Labs (YC F26).

Our family spent nearly two decades caring for loved ones at home. Now we’re building the technology we wish we’d had.

More independence for your parents. More of your time together spent just being family.

evidence.text:
The new Voice Mode is awesome, thanks for shipping it, 
@OpenAI
 !

Today I asked ChatGPT (mobile app) to search Slack in Voice Mode. It said it couldn’t access connectors. I typed the exact same request in the same conversation, and it worked immediately. I believe it's because Voice Mode and Chat run in different execution environments, which would explain the difference in capabilities.

Later, I learned from a friend that if I want a voice-first workflow from my phone with connected tools, I should be using Work/Codex with Remote.  So there is a (not great) workaround for now. 

The surprising part was that ChatGPT couldn’t help me arrive at that conclusion either even after I asked it to look up the docs. That feels like a documentation and product discoverability gap more than anything else.

I’d love to see these experiences converge over time. In the meantime, making the differences between Chat, Voice, Work/Codex, and Remote much more explicit in docs would make the product significantly easier to understand and use.

Later, I learned from a friend that if I want a voice-first workflow from my phone with connected tools, I should be using Work/Codex with Remote.  So there is a (not great) workaround for now. 

The surprising part was that ChatGPT couldn’t help me arrive at that conclusion either even after I asked it to look up the docs. That feels like a documentation and product discoverability gap more than anything else.

I’d love to see these experiences converge over time. In the meantime, making the differences between Chat, Voice, Work/Codex, and Remote much more explicit in docs would make the product significantly easier to understand and use.

evidence.text:
“Fishing for Dreams”
36 in. x 12 in.
acrylic on canvas
2025

a slightly older painting (finished in January), this piece embodies the wonders of childhood and the pursuit of chasing fantastical dreams, represented by each koi fish - escapes, hopes, and realms that stay ever so slightly out of reach. 

as a kid, we all wanted to be something - a dragon, a ninja, a popstar, a princess, an artist - but we grow up and must assume responsibility, assume function in our capitalistic world, assume our own worth by the value society places on our careers. and with this impending coming-of-age, our dreams escape us, until we forget and they fade.

evidence.title:
Procter & Gamble took more than $200 million a year out of its costs by redrawing which plant makes what.

In 1993 P&G made Olay, Cover Girl and Max Factor alongside Tide and Pampers, in plants across the United States and Canada. Each category had grown its own plants and shipping patterns over decades.

The company set up a study to ask one question across the whole network: which products should be made where, and shipped from where, to serve every customer at the lowest total cost. A team from P&G and the University of Cincinnati built integer-programming and network models and linked them to a mapping system, so managers could see each option on a map and apply their own judgment before deciding.

What changed:
- the number of North American plants cut by almost 20 percent
- over $200 million a year in pretax savings
- a finalist for the 1996 Franz Edelman Award, operations research's top prize for real-world results

It took a company of P&G's size a dedicated team and a study that began in 1993 and was still being implemented in 1997. That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a network of 3 plants or 30, built in weeks on the data a manufacturer already has.

If your plants still run on the footprint they inherited, we'd like to hear how you decide what moves where.

founders@operatechnologies.com

evidence.title:
Adding a £3 booking fee cost the AA almost £5 million.

The AA's driving schools left the mandatory fee out of the upfront price...

New customers only saw it at checkout, after choosing lessons, picking times and entering their details. 

More than 80,000 learners paid it, around £760,000 in total. All of it is now being refunded.

On top of that, the UK competition regulator fined the AA £4.2 million, roughly five and a half times what the fee brought in. 

The fine actually started at £7 million but the AA got 40% off for admitting the breach and agreeing not to appeal.

The fee was small, but more than 80,000 people were shown an incomplete price... for eight months.

If you add any mandatory fee, check that it appears in the first price customers see.

We ranked it alongside nine much larger 2026 penalties in The Ledger from Index Law. Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
McCormick, the US spice giant, is buying a business more than twice its own size.

Unilever's foods business, which includes Hellmann's and Knorr, is valued at $44.8 billion. When talks began, McCormick's whole market value was about $14.5 billion.

It can't pay that in cash. Unilever gets $15.7 billion in cash and the rest in McCormick shares. 

The deal is structured as a "Reverse Morris Trust" so it's tax-free in the US for Unilever and its shareholders. That leaves McCormick's own shareholders with 35% of the company they're buying into.

A structure like that needs specialists. McCormick's lawyers are Cleary Gottlieb, and their team includes US and UK tax, capital markets and antitrust partners alongside the M&A lead.

It's also a team McCormick knew. Cleary advised on its $4.2 billion purchase of Reckitt Benckiser's food brands in 2017, which brought it French's mustard and Frank's RedHot. Hogan Lovells, its other firm, worked on its 2016 bid for Premier Foods, the UK food group.

This week's Ledger shows who acted on ten of 2026's biggest deals and which firms keep coming back.

Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
8 US states sued OpenAI on 14 October over ChatGPT and children. So is ChatGPT safe for your kids?

ChatGPT does have teen protections: parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate settings for users under 18. But they only switch on if ChatGPT knows it's talking to a teenager. 

No age check is needed to use the website. OpenAI relies on a system that guesses a user's age, and a news report cited in Iowa's petition said that at one point it treated minors as adults about 12% of the time.

The states don't have to prove ChatGPT harmed a particular child. They're suing under consumer-protection law, the sam law used against misleading adverts. 

So what the states are suing over is whether OpenAI's safety claims matched the product. Iowa alone seeks up to $40,000 per violation.

OpenAI says it has "built industry-leading age-specific protections" and that "no system can be perfect". It hasn't filed a response, and nothing has been decided yet.

If you're a parent, the protections only work if your child is identified as a teen, so set up parental controls yourself. If you build a product children use, "safe by default" has to be true by default.

We break down both sides in this week's Index Brief.

Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
Wild claim, but our evals back it up: for realistic human conversation, you don't need frontier compute to get frontier quality.

We used the current SOTA models of GPT-5.5 (Extra High) and Opus 4.8 (Max) to grade >400k simulated scenario replies against our internal evaluation framework. The winner for our use case? Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite. Post pipeline optimization, it achieved near previous generation SOTA (Opus 4.7) performance at ~1/300th the cost and ~100x the speed.

Why? It's a systems problem, not a model-size one. The attached diagram shows how it fits together: one streamed call for the live reply, while coaching, scoring, memory, and ending logic run async beside it. The offline loop turns every rehearsal into corpus → eval → tuning. That compounding practice is the real moat. You can easily swap an underlying model anytime, but you can't easily swap accumulated data.

We also incorporated privacy from day one: all conversations are de-identified & aggregate-only. No live users yet, but with the help of synthetic data, we have a data pipeline that's already sharpening itself.

Frontier quality is a systems bet.

#quippy #ai #llms #tech

evidence.text:
Never abandon the thing you're building mid-flight.

Because walking away doesn't give you clarity-
it gives you a ghost.

A quiet voice that follows you into every side project,
every pivot, every "new idea"...

whispering that you bailed on the one thing
you actually believed was real.

And if you quit on the product you felt in your gut was right-
the agent, the tool, the thing you stayed up building at midnight-
it doesn't vanish.

It just becomes the benchmark you measure every future attempt against.

So keep shipping.
Not because it's going well.
But because you owe yourself the answer to what this thing actually becomes.

In June 2020 after one my previous startup failed, I learned 10 lessons from my ex-co-founder:

1. Grit — When he set his eye on something simple, NOTHING stopped him
2. Frugality — Ruthless about costs he understood
3. Hard choices — Could fire people without blinking
4. Fake it till you make it — Sold features that didn't exist yet
5. Cold calling — Scripts, flowcharts, prepared rebuttals
6. Confidence — Held his own with VIP investors
7. Perspective shift — "You're doing THEM a favor by selling"
8. Energy transfer — Used mood to control rooms
9. Meeting outcomes — Planned conclusions in advance
10. End on highs — Always planned something nice at day's end

We were terrible decision-makers at the time.

But I learned more from him than any book.

Even failures in building a company teaches you something.

evidence.title:
Zara added an estimated $586M in revenue over two years, using stock it already had.

Until 2006, it decided how many units of each item and size to send to its 1,500 stores like this: every week, store managers requested quantities, and a team at the warehouse reduced those requests to fit what was left in stock.

Zara then worked with Felipe Caro (UCLA) and Jérémie Gallien (MIT Sloan) to replace that step with a demand forecast and an optimization model that splits the warehouse stock across stores, size by size.

They tested it against a control group before rolling it out. Sales went up 3 to 4 percent, about $233M of extra revenue in 2007 and $353M in 2008.

The stores and the clothes stayed the same. What changed was the decision about where each unit goes.

A lot of retailers still make that call with store requests and spreadsheets. If that's your team, we'd like to hear how you do it today.

evidence.title:
Imagine you’ve raised $1 million. Another investor offers $500k on the same terms.

How much of your company have you now promised?

On a post-money SAFE with a $10 million valuation cap, the first $1 million represents about 10%.

The extra $500k adds another 5%.

You’ve raised $1.5 million and committed an estimated 15%, before the next round’s new investment. That assumes the cap determines conversion and no other adjustments apply.

Now suppose new investors buy 20% of the company in your next round.

If the SAFE holders invest no more money and nothing else changes, their combined stake goes from 15% to 12%.

That drop keeps going from 15% to around 6% assuming dilution every round if the company IPOs...

We explain the calculation and the wording behind it in The Small Print from Index Law. Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
Two investors each offer $5 million for 20% of your company.

Later, the company sells with $20 million left for shareholders. One investor receives $5 million. The other receives $8 million.

The difference is one clause. The first has a 1x non-participating preference: it takes its $5 million back or converts to 20% of the proceeds ($4 million), whichever is greater. The second is fully participating: $5 million back first, then 20% of the remaining $15 million.

That investor owns 20% of the company and takes 40% of the sale.

Neither term is deceiving. They're just two different bargains with the same numbers. The preference decides what everyone gets out, so model the payouts at several exit values before you choose between offers.

We walk through this and three other clauses that move in a Series A in our latest edition of The Small Print. Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
Tesla sold Full Self-Driving packages for between $3,000 and $15,000. 

From late 2016, its Autopilot page said every car had the hardware needed for full self-driving.

California buyers sued over that sentence. A federal judge certified classes covering more than 3,800 people on Tesla's own data. 

After May 2017: only buyers who opted out of Tesla's arbitration agreement could still be in court. Across more than seven years of sales, that was at least 212 people.

On 16 October the Ninth Circuit vacated the class orders anyway. Buyers weren't required to visit the Autopilot page to complete a purchase, so the court wouldn't assume every class member saw the statement.

The full breakdown is in this week's Index Brief. Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title: Going so deep into model behaviour has given us a really unique perspective on the exact capabilities that the current models lack. Lots of tokens and late nights later, we see the
evidence.text:
Going so deep into model behaviour has given us a really unique perspective on the exact capabilities that the current models lack. Lots of tokens and late nights later, we see these things even with the latest models:

1. The notice-act gap - Similar to the findings in 
https://
openai.com/index/introduc
ing-genebench-pro/
… we see that the models are able to notice information and even predict a strategy that would increase performance, but fail to take the actions necessary to actually implement that strategy. We even see "experimentation" in notes/reasoning, but that doesn't work well without actually implementing the experiments. 3 out of 26 times that Astra's notes mention buying more to close the gap, it buys the same or LESS for that day.

2. Impact on the environment -  The frontier models consistently underestimate the impact of their actions on the environment and don't recognise the second-order effects. In SMB Bench we see that models consistently treat a short delivery to a customer as a one-day cost. A customer who gets shorted quietly orders less from then on. Across the runs where this happens, a model connected its customers' falling orders to its own short deliveries in only ~21%, and in just ~17% of those did it then protect every account within three days.

Noticing a problem, changing behaviour and actually improving the outcome turn out to be three separate skills that no frontier model has gotten correct in combination in these long horizon tasks.

evidence.text:
Day 399 of building

agent37.com 

I researched co-founder success rates.

The finding:

Remote co-founders with no pre-existing relationship = 10X harder to succeed.

I learned this the hard way.

Long ago, I met a potential co-founder online.

After 1 month, red flags emerged:
• Both of us wanted to be CEO
• Different location preferences
• No willingness to relocate long-term from either of us.

I ended it.

It wasn't pretty.

Maybe I should've asked the hard questions earlier.

But I saved us both years on something doomed to fail.

Now I know:

Do the compatibility exercise in Week 1, not Month 3.

Uncomfortable questions early > messy breakups later.

evidence.title: “In Another Life”
evidence.text:
“In Another Life”
24 in. x 48 in.
oil on canvas 
2025

“right person, wrong time” - a saying for the relationships that don’t work out. caught up in the pressing matters of life, career, the world - each person waits for their prospective trains, on two different platforms, on their way to part ways. but in another life, where there are no responsibilities, worries, or fears, the two remain as one - on a singular track together. they bask in a fantastical world, of magic and wonder, free and joyful. in another life, there is no “wrong time”but just “right person.”
