evidence.title:
Google cut the energy one of its data centres spent on cooling by up to 40 percent by letting a model choose the settings.

A data centre's cooling plant is a set of pumps, chillers and cooling towers. Which ones to run, and at what setpoints, changes with the weather and the computing load. Operators used to set them by formula and experience.

In 2016 DeepMind trained neural networks on years of sensor data from the site to predict energy use for each option and recommend the best one. Operators applied the recommendations by hand.

Tested by switching the recommendations on and off:
- up to 40 percent less energy for cooling
- 15 percent lower PUE overhead, the lowest PUE the site had ever seen

In 2018 Google let the system control the cooling directly, under the operators' supervision. Every five minutes it takes a snapshot from thousands of sensors, picks an action, checks it against safety constraints in the cloud, and the local system checks it again. Operators can take back control at any time. Savings went from about 12 percent at launch to around 30 percent on average within months.

Google has never said what that is worth in dollars. Business Insider's estimate at the time: tens, or even hundreds, of millions of dollars if applied across all of its data centres.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same idea for a plant or a fleet, built in weeks on the data the operation already has.

How does your team set the operating points it adjusts every day?

founders@operatechnologies.com

evidence.title:
DiDi, China's dominant ride-hailing company, raised $4.4 billion in its 2021 IPO.

Two days later, China's cyberspace regulator opened a cybersecurity review. Within a week, its app had been pulled from Chinese app stores and the shares had fallen as much as 25%.

Investors sued. They alleged the prospectus left out that Chinese regulators had warned DiDi not to list until it complied with data laws. DiDi has said it didn't know before listing that a probe was coming. 

In June 2026, a US court approved a $740 million settlement, about 17% of the money the IPO raised. DiDi admitted no wrongdoing...

Why so large, for investors who bought in a three-week window? Investors who buy in an IPO can sue over a misleading prospectus without proving anyone intended to deceive them. The court let those claims proceed in 2024.

When you sell shares, anything material you knew and left out of the document becomes the company's risk.

We ranked ten of the largest US securities settlements in The Ledger from Index Law. Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
A jury found Arm broke its license with Qualcomm. It awarded Qualcomm $2.

One dollar for breaching the license. One dollar for interfering with Qualcomm's deal with Meta. Qualcomm brings in about $1,400 of revenue every second.

Why so little? The jury was told damages must put Qualcomm where it would have been if Arm had performed, and that it "must not speculate or guess". If a breach was proved but the loss couldn't be quantified, it could award nominal damages of $1. Qualcomm's lawyer had told the jury the Meta deal lost $170 million in value. That became $1.

The real money was never the jury's to give. Qualcomm wants up to five years of royalty-free use of Arm's technology under a clause in their contracts. Reuters says that is potentially worth billions. Arm, the British chip-design company whose technology Qualcomm builds on, says the clause is an unenforceable penalty. In its words, it's "one-size-fits-all": the same five years whether Arm withholds a few test materials or everything it owes. The judge decides that, not the jury.

Proving the other side broke the contract and proving what it cost you are separate jobs. A remedy that doesn't scale with the breach invites exactly the argument Arm is making.

We break down the verdict, the clause and what we would have wanted settled at signing in this week's Index Brief.

Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
SpaceX's IPO priced at $135 a share. The underwriting banks paid $134.10.

Multiply that 90 cents by all 638.9m shares sold and you get about $575m. The underwriting agreement points to about $500m.

The difference is in how the agreement prices two groups of shares. Section 2 sets the $134.10 purchase price for the 555.6m "firm" shares the banks committed to buy. The banks also had an option over 83.3m additional shares, and the agreement prices those "at the Public Offering Price", which is $135. They exercised the option in full.

Extend the 90 cents to the option shares and the spread is overstated by about $75m. The terms were all in the public filing. This is a reading error anyone could make, not a claim that SpaceX or its banks made one.

In this edition of The Small Print, we go through the agreement clause by clause, including the expense caps and the costs that remain even if a deal fails.

evidence.title:
More than 400 former Apple employees now work at OpenAI. Apple can't sue over that. So it's suing over the job interviews.

In California, non-competes are void, "no matter how narrowly tailored". Federal trade secrets law adds that a court can't stop someone taking a job, and can't restrict their new role "merely on the information the person knows".

So knowing a lot about Apple isn't enough. Apple has to show what was taken, or what candidates were asked to bring. It says OpenAI's hardware chief, a 24-year Apple veteran, asked a candidate to "bring some parts [she] worked on". OpenAI says he meant products that had already shipped, and a lot now rests on what that one word means.

OpenAI was willing to agree not to use Apple's information, to stop any current use and to preserve evidence. It refused the two requests that would let Apple check: forensic inspection of its devices and accounts, and a search of its network.

On 13 October the judge ordered OpenAI to hand over its interview checklists, guides and scripts within 14 days. Three days later, he approved an agreement under which OpenAI won't use the alleged secrets and will collect images of 14 employees' devices. Apple's injunction motion was declared moot. 

Nobody has won, and OpenAI denies the allegations.

We break down both sides, and the interview rules we would have wanted in place, in this week's Index Brief.

Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title: EveryApp (YC F26) - Make every app open source
evidence.text:
TL;DR: EveryApp is an open-source app store and the cloud to run it. Install an open-source app or have your agent build your own. Everything runs in your own Cloudflare account, behind one secure sign-in.

[video]
The problem
SaaS is dead. Per-seat pricing sucks. Blah blah blah.
Actually though, 99% of businesses need the same set of basic tools and they want them to work well with their agents. 

Solution

We’re going to build open source versions of every SaaS, then put them all on EveryApp. As coding agents keep getting better, we can take on more ambitious products. 

Right now, we’re just launching the self-hosted version for people already comfortable using agents. But, when the hosted platform is launched, this will be a magical experience for everyone. Every product you could ever want, accessible to you and your agent without even needing to sign up for a new service. 

EveryApp
EveryApp makes two things easy: hosting open-source apps, and hosting custom apps you build with your agent. Your team accesses and manages them through the EveryApp Gateway.
Secure by default
Every request passes through the Gateway. Apps have no public address. 
Connect an API once. Apps ask for access, and the Gateway makes the call, so no app ever holds your keys.
Put it behind Cloudflare Access.
Scales from zero to infinity
Fully serverless, in your own Cloudflare account.
Apps cost $0 if they aren’t used. 
Scale up to Cloudflare’s scale if needed.
$5/month for Cloudflare Paid Plan which can host thousands of apps.
Standardized
You don’t need to think about infra. Everything must run Cloudflare’s cloud primitives like KV and R2. 
When building something new, use our preferred tech stack and component library so you don’t need to define patterns yourself. 
OpenSEO & more
I first launched EveryApp in January. It was a framework with no useful apps, nobody had a reason to trust it, and building an app on it was still hard.

So, I set out to build a standalone product that was compelling. That ended up being OpenSEO which now has over 24,000 GitHub stars and thousands of customers who love it.

Coding agents got a lot better since then too. Building an app on EveryApp is now something you can do in a few hours while multitasking. 

Last week we forked some popular open source projects to get them running on EveryApp: OpenCRM, OpenAnalytics and Agentic Inbox. Over the coming months we'll ship many more, so you don't have to build apps from scratch anymore.

Team
Ben Senescu - Prev. Senior SWE at Klaviyo & Founding Eng. building Agents for Compliance

evidence.title:
Your health insurance comes from your job. Nobody designed it that way.

In 1942 Congress froze wages to control inflation. Employers couldn't legally pay more, but fringe benefits didn't count as wages. So they competed on health insurance instead.

A year later the IRS ruled employer-paid coverage wasn't taxable income. Regulators called the cost negligible.

That negligible cost is now a $27,000 family plan.

Our Founder and CEO Nick Taranto breaks down how that accident became the system ▶️

evidence.title:
Coca-Cola Enterprises cut its delivery costs by $45 million a year by changing how its dispatchers build their routes.

Its direct-store delivery fleet was about 10,000 trucks. Every day, more than 300 dispatchers decided which stops went on which truck, and in what order.

In 2004 and 2005 CCE put an optimization model under that decision, developed with the routing company ORTEC and Tilburg University. The dispatchers did not go away: more than 300 of them still plan the routes every day, now with the model. CCE moved over gradually instead of switching overnight; the write-up singles that out as the notable part of the project.

What changed:
- about $45 million a year in lower delivery cost
- fewer miles driven, so less fuel burned
- major improvements in customer service, reported alongside the savings
- the same approach was then rolled out to other Coca-Cola bottlers and to beer distributors, among them Heineken, Carlsberg and InBev

It was a finalist for the 2007 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research for results in the real world.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of routing model for a fleet of 20 trucks or 20,000, built in weeks on the data a distributor already has.

If your dispatchers still build tomorrow's routes by hand, we'd like to hear how.

founders@operatechnologies.com

evidence.title:
A yacht broker is suing the founder of Revolut for €17.5 million over the purchase of his €350 million superyacht.

It says it found the yacht, arranged an inspection and helped produce an offer before being left out of the final deal.

His family office says the claim is without merit and will be defended.

The case comes down to two questions:

> What was the broker actually hired to do?
> And did its work cause the final sale, even after the yacht changed owners?

Clear terms on payment, direct purchases and ownership changes could have made that much easier to answer.

We just published the full breakdown of the case. Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
You send a potential partner the technical plans for a new product. Both sides sign an NDA.

The partner stores the plans securely and never shares them outside its team. Then it uses them to build a competing feature.

Nothing has leaked. You may still have a contract dispute.

An NDA usually makes two promises. One is to keep your information confidential. The other is to use it only for an agreed purpose. 

In Common Paper's standard mutual NDA, the second is a single line: the recipient must "use Confidential Information solely for the Purpose". The Purpose is whatever the parties write on the cover page.

If that says "evaluating a potential integration", the recipient has permission to evaluate. It hasn't necessarily been given permission to build a rival product from your plans. The NDA doesn't grant it a license to your IP either.

We go through it, and three other parts of an NDA nobody negotiates, in The Small Print from Index Law. Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
Imagine your software company has signed a $60,000 a year customer contract. You looked through & negotiated the liability cap carefully.

Then the customer forwards a lawsuit. Another company says your software infringes its intellectual property, and the customer wants you to handle it.

Well, there's a big chance the cap you negotiated may not apply to that claim at all.

Most software contracts have two separate promises about money.

1. The liability cap is the most you'll pay if something goes wrong between you and the customer. Here, maybe a year's fees.
2. The indemnity is a promise to protect the customer if someone else sues them because of your product. You pay their lawyers, and any settlement or damages.

Many standard contracts list the indemnity as an exception to the cap. So a cap you negotiated hard can leave the most expensive claim with no limit at all, because a lawsuit like this can cost far more than $60,000.

In The Small Print from Index Law, we follow one lawsuit through a standard software contract: what's covered, who runs the defense, and which limits actually apply.

Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
An OpenAI engineer was arrested nine days after staff found a thumb-sized recording device plugged into a television in an executive conference room.

So if something went wrong inside your company tomorrow, could your own AI tools' logs help you find who did it? In this case, prosecutors say that is largely how the trail was built.

According to the FBI's affidavit, the engineer had asked an OpenAI productivity agent which rooms seat six or more, what was on a room's calendar and where leadership meets. A ChatGPT account in his wife's name, which prosecutors link to him through shared identifiers, logged prompts about building a continuous audio recorder and about the device's unique details. OpenAI says it also used its own models to work out who had planted the device.

He is charged with endeavouring to intercept oral conversations. The memory card could not be read, and on the face of the statute the government does not need a recovered recording. Nothing has been proved. He denies the allegations through his lawyers and is presumed innocent.

We break down the charge, the contested attribution and what companies should settle in the first 72 hours in this week's Index Brief.

Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title: Funding is overrated. 3 things that matter way more when you’re planning a startup 👇
evidence.text:
Funding is overrated. 3 things that matter way more when you’re planning a startup 👇

1. Your co-founder
Not just a co-founder - the right one. Shared conviction, complementary skills, and someone you’d still want in the trenches at 2 am on month 18.

2. Execution > idea

Ideas are cheap. Everyone has one in the shower. Building it, shipping it, iterating on it when the market punches back — that’s the whole game.

3. Cutting through the noise
Everyone has advice. Investors, podcasts, threads, your uncle. Learn to listen, filter, and trust the signal in your gut. Fail fast, learn faster.

Money follows momentum. Build the momentum first. 🚀

evidence.text:
Day 391.

I keep seeing founders brag about running ten AI coding sessions at once and juggling massive parallel workflows.

Maybe I am just not that smart, but I realized this week that context switching is actually killing my productivity. When I am tackling a truly hard engineering problem, I cannot afford to tab away for two minutes and expect to retain the context in my brain.

I stopped trying to multitask. I pick the one hard task that actually moves the needle, finish it, and then move on. It feels much slower, but more actually gets done.

32% reported significant personal stress from managing costs and renewals. 25% said it strained their own household finances. 23% reduced contributions to their own retirement. 14% took a cut or freeze to their own pay.

The benefits line has a person attached to it, and it's usually the person who signed off on it.

evidence.title: SPM Builds Defense Compliant Battery Packs - YC Launch
evidence.text:
At SPM, we’re building the highest-performance, defense-compliant battery packs and power export systems for dual-use applications. 

We’ve identified a huge gap in energy/mobility battery pack supply chain. 

Mobilizing energy is a national priority, with electronic warfare and field computing requiring increasing power. Designed, manufactured, and put into low-volume production in 1/4 of the time of most incumbent battery manufacturers— SPM is filling the gap that both startups and major primes are experiencing. America needs more reliable battery pack suppliers that produce high quality, safe and reliable packs, with non-FEOC components. That’s how we’ve always done it. 

We started directly selling our battery pack and power system capability to customers in August 2026 and went from pre-orders, to $421,000 in one month, with a pipeline of almost $1M for the remainder of the year. We are slated to become a prime contractor in 2027, but we have a much more rapid strategy right now - sell to prime contractors who needs packs - and this strategy absolutely works. 

Our team is scaling production capacity in Pittsburgh Pennsylvania - we’re already fully booked for the remainder of 2026. Because our entire battery packs are vertically integrated except the cell, we can develop custom battery packs with a patented design methodology that doesn’t require specialized manufacturing equipment. After design and low-volume production starts, any shop with a spot welder can acquire parts and finish the assembly. In the end, this strengthens domestic battery pack supply chain integrity with rapidly scalable battery packs that use a common module form factor. 

Super Powers Mobility started out developing high-voltage powertrain systems for light off-road vehicles and late this summer we shifted to power systems for energy mobilization and mobility products like UGVs, UAS, and USVs. Since switching focus, SPM has joined 4 federal contracts to supply batteries and power electronics systems. 

We are expanding our team! https://www.linkedin.com/company/superpowersmobility/jobs 

You can also check our YC Jobs page. 

Need batteries or a custom vehicle development program?
 
Reach us at info@spm.fun or check our website below.
 
Government/enterprise website - www.spm.us

evidence.title: "I just need the form filled in."
evidence.text:
"I just need the form filled in."

That phrase arrives in almost every early conversation. It is one of the clearest signals in visa work.

It rarely means carelessness. It is a map of how the applicant understands the process, and the map is missing most of the territory.

The belief underneath it is simple: the visa application is a form problem. In practice, it is a consistency problem across an entire document set.

A Schengen application runs across seven separate sources: passport, employment letter, bank statement, flight itinerary, hotel booking, travel insurance, and the form itself.

Every one of those documents has to say the same thing about the same person.

A contradiction between any two of them surfaces in review. The system is built to enforce precision.

This is why extraction accuracy matters long before the form is touched. If the data read from a passport does not match the employment letter or the bank statement, the inconsistency is already in the file.

The check worth running first:

Open the passport and the employment letter side by side. Look at name spelling, date of birth, and nationality.

If those three do not align exactly, the form is the last thing to think about. →

Veeza AI reads your passport, fills your visa form, and checks consistency across your full document set before anything is submitted. A real visa expert reviews every detail too.

Start your application at veeza.ai.

evidence.text:
If your competitor uses the same AI model you do, what's left to compete on?

Three leaders in our Future of Marketing series agreed.

Scott Neuman says to assume your competition has the same tools and the same insight, then ask who knows the customer best.

Bruce Millard says AI will 10x a good idea and turn a bad one into 10x more noise.

Setareh M. said it best: "The moat really isn't the model. I think it's the customer intelligence that you're bringing into your team."

From a sales perspective, we know that whichever rep knows their customer best will likely win the deal. 

What does your team know about your buyers that a competitor couldn't get from a chatbot?

evidence.title:
Kellogg has planned production for its cereal plants with an optimization model it installed in 1990 and still ran every Sunday morning a decade later.

Five plants, seven distribution centers, about 15 co-packers. In cereal alone: 600+ SKUs, roughly 90 production lines and 180 packaging lines. Every week the same question: which product runs on which line, in which plant, and where the cases ship.

Before that, each plant planned for itself, with spreadsheets and MRP software. In 1987 Kellogg decided that no longer worked for a product line that size and built the Kellogg Planning System with two operations researchers from the Naval Postgraduate School: a linear program that plans 30 weeks ahead and reruns each Sunday. Planners turn its output into the detailed schedules, and managers still adjust what doesn't fit the plant floor.

What changed:
- an estimated $4.5 million less production, inventory and distribution cost in 1995, once true plant costs were in the model
- a monthly version for plant budgets and capacity decisions, which guided a consolidation with projected savings of $35 to $40 million a year
- still in use more than ten years after it was built, when the team wrote it up in 2001

It took Kellogg years and a dedicated team to get there. That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of production plan, built in weeks on your data.

If your weekly production plan still lives in a spreadsheet or old softwares, we'd like to hear how you build it.

founders@operatechnologies.com

evidence.title:
The ultimate luxury in business is the space to think.

Every day, you operate at the intersection of digital chaos and physical reality. You act as the bridge between late-night threads, delayed dispatches, and sudden market pivots. You are carrying a million unstructured variables in your head.

The industry’s standard response to this complexity is generalized AI. But massive models trained on the internet cannot comprehend the specific, living physics of your operations.

To solve this, we had to build something else entirely.

Welcome to Evokoa.

Founded by Dalton, Dale Ng and Damien L.
Evokoa introduces a fundamentally new architecture built from the ground up: one that creates a living model of your world.

Evokoa is designed to let complexity structure itself. It autonomously fuses unstructured human context (isolated files, scattered conversations, and split-second decisions) directly with live IoT telemetry and real-time environmental state.

When the machine is finally capable of holding the complexity, the cognitive load lifts. You get to step back, see the whole board, and actually do the work you were meant to do.

Pioneer batch 2 is open. Build your world: evokoa.com

Here is what Gell-Mann amnesia is: You read an arti
evidence.text:
I think of Gell-Mann Amnesia as one of the most important cognitive biases to be aware of and correct as you interact with AI. 

Here is what Gell-Mann amnesia is: You read an article on something you know well and spot everything that's wrong. Then you turn the page and trust the next article completely. That's Gell-Mann amnesia. 

AI has the same problem. A compliance expert reads an AI response and finds the errors. Most people accept the answer. Don't just do that. 

That's why you need a system that is built on expert data. So that the system can use tests and evaluations to ensure there are not incorrect conclusions or data.

Day 369

I used to think becoming a millionaire required luck.

Then I read this Quora thread where actual millionaires answered: "What would you do if you lost everything?"

Every single one was confident they'd rebuild.

Not hopeful. CONFIDENT.

That's when I realized:

Wealth isn't an event. It's a skill.

If Elon Musk started over today, he'd be rich again in years. Not because of luck, because of how his brain works.

So I stopped wishing for luck and started training my brain.

8 years later: I'm not a millionaire yet (halfway there thanks to FAANG jobs).

But I know I will be. And I think I know how...

evidence.title: “Bruises and Blooms”
evidence.text:
“Bruises and Blooms”
16 in. x 40 in.
oil on canvas 
2025

when i ended my long-term relationship last winter, i got to experience heartbreak for the first time (yay!!); quite painful, rather depressing, but also very transformative. this painting was inspired first by that experience, but then by the idea of growth from pain. from a stab wound that feels unbearably permanent, flowers blossom and glow, symbolizing the beauty in the process of healing, of rebuilding, of emergence. though he cries in protest and pain, he does not yet see the flurry of fauna blooming from his back.

evidence.title:
When a snowstorm cancelled 112 flights at Newark, Continental Airlines had its crews re-planned in three and a half minutes.

A cancelled flight strands crews. Pilots and flight attendants end up in the wrong city, over their legal hours, or out of position for tomorrow. Putting 4,000 pilots and 8,000 flight attendants back on schedule used to be done by hand, partly by phoning airports to find out who was where. After one storm in 1993 Continental, in its own words, completely lost control.

From 1994 Continental and CALEB Technologies built CrewSolver: an optimization system that reassigns crews after a disruption, inside every regulation, contract rule and quality-of-life constraint, in minutes instead of hours.

What changed, by Continental's estimate:
- about $40 million saved in 2001 across four major disruptions
- the Houston flood: a re-plan that would have taken 72 hours by hand was done in eight, crews notified included
- September 11: 1,600 crew pairings rerouted in under 17 minutes

It won the 2002 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of re-planning model for a plant or a fleet when a machine or a driver drops out, built in weeks on the data the operation already has.

When something breaks in your operation, how long until the plan is whole again?

founders@operatechnologies.com

evidence.title:
TNT Express cut €207 million of cost in four years by putting models under decisions its depots had always made by hand.

TNT moved about 4.7 million parcels, documents and freight items a week to over 200 countries, through depots, hubs, trucks and planes. Until 2005 that network was designed and its routes planned without mathematical support.

That year it launched the Global Optimization programme: one model for where depots and hubs should sit, one for the line-haul schedule between them, one for the pickup-and-delivery rounds. It also put more than 150 managers through a two-year in-house academy, so the people running the depots could run the models themselves.

What changed, by TNT's count:
- more than €207 million in savings and benefits between 2008 and 2011
- 200 network optimisation projects in 2011 alone
- depot locations, line-haul and local routes all decided on the same data

It won the 2012 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

TNT Express no longer exists as a brand, but the lesson does: the models mattered less than teaching the operators to use them. That's how we work at OpEra: a model built in weeks on the data a depot already has, run by the people who run the depot.

If your line-haul schedule is still set by whoever has run it longest, we'd like to hear how.

evidence.title:
After Amazon split its US fulfillment network into eight regions, the distance between its sites and customers fell 15% and its cost to serve each unit went down for the first time since 2018, by more than $0.45 a unit in the US, by Amazon's count.

Until then Amazon ran the US as one flexible national network. By 2021, the network's rapid growth had made transportation disproportionately complex, which Amazon's team says raised costs while slowing delivery. Underneath sits a decision every distributor faces at a smaller scale: which buildings hold which products, and which customers each building serves.

Amazon's own operations research team spent about a year and a half on the redesign: drawing the region boundaries, modeling the network, and weighing how much inventory each region needs against how fast it can deliver, along with the software and operational changes to run it. The principle was to match demand with capacity within each region, so that the eight regions are connected but largely self-sufficient. After a pilot, the new network was fully deployed by March 2023.

What changed, by Amazon's count:
- 15% less distance between sites and customers
- 12% fewer middle-mile touchpoints
- Orders filled within the customer's region up from 62% to 76%
- More than $0.45 per unit saved in the US, the first drop in cost-to-serve per unit since 2018, while delivery got faster

It was a finalist for the 2025 Franz Edelman Award.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of network model for a distributor with four warehouses deciding which one serves which customers, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team ships each order from wherever the stock happens to be, we'd like to hear how you decide what to hold where.

evidence.title:

A retired teacher needed to pay his granddaughter’s college fee, so he asked his bank’s AI assistant to break a sav
evidence.text:
An AI agent did everything right and still let a customer down.

A retired teacher needed to pay his granddaughter’s college fee, so he asked his bank’s AI assistant to break a savings deposit early and move the money to his account.

The AI found the right deposit, closed it, moved the exact amount and told him it was done.

But it never mentioned the penalty for closing early, and it never asked if he still wanted to go ahead, even though a short overdraft could have covered the fee for much less.

And the tests companies run before putting agents in front of customers would still mark this as a pass, because most of them only check the final records.

A database remembers what an agent changed, but it has no trace of the warning it never gave or the question it never asked.

On a banking test with 1,000 tasks, checking only the final records made every model look 6.5 to 12 points better than it really was.

And that’s a big blind spot, because an agent can get every record right and still fail the person it’s working for.

So when you test an agent, check what it should have said and asked along the way, as well as what it changed at the end.

Full breakdown here

They don’t know what changed.

Take a warehouse. A cold-storage shipment gets moved t
evidence.text:
Most AI agents aren’t ready to run live operations yet. And the reason is surprisingly basic.

They don’t know what changed.

Take a warehouse. A cold-storage shipment gets moved three times in one morning, and the AI reads every one of those updates. Then someone asks where the shipment is, and the AI points to an older scan. So the driver walks up to an empty bay.

The AI wasn’t missing any information. It just couldn’t tell which update was the latest.

Ai2 built a test for exactly this, called StateBench. On its longest tests, four of the top AI models got it right 13% of the time or less.

So the industry is judging agents on the wrong thing. We keep asking how much they can read, search and remember, but for real work the question is whether they know what’s true right now.

Until that’s fixed, an agent running live operations is a risk.
We broke down the full study in our latest blog.

I discovered my #1 productivity hack by accident:

ARTIFICIAL CONSTRAINTS.

Here's what happened:

I had a whole week to finish a task. Was procrastinating. YouTube. Food. BS.

Then my girlfriend texted: "Coming over in 2 hours for sandwiches."

Suddenly I NEEDED to finish before she arrived.

And I did. Easily.

The insight:

Your brain doesn't respond to "I should work."

It responds to "I MUST finish before [undeniable event]."

Now I schedule "obstruction events" deliberately:
- Calls
- Gym sessions
- Dinners

Work expands to fill time.

So shrink the time.

Rippling doesn't publish pricing. Every quote is custom, based on your headcount, core platform, and the modules you add.

That means two similar companies can end up paying very different amounts without knowing it.

The published starting point is $8 per employee per month plus a $35 base fee. Modules add their own per-employee charges, contracts run for 12 months, and some users report being billed based on their original headcount even after their team shrinks.

For benefits, Rippling gives you access to large-group plans through its carrier relationships. But it doesn't shop the full market at renewal or show you the risk score carriers use to price your workforce.

See the full breakdown, including the costs users report: https://lnkd.in/eyy_MG_3

evidence.title:
“When I qualified as a lawyer we used to bill in 5-minute units”

When our Senior Founding Advisor Dominic Raab qualified as a lawyer, firms billed in five-minute units. Every five minutes had to be accounted for.

“It shows what a producer-oriented sector it was. We want to turn that around.”

That means redesigning legal services around the client, without outsourcing accountability to AI.

At Index Law, AI handles routine work where confidence is high and gives lawyers the best possible information everywhere else. But a human remains the last mile in every case, applying judgement and making the final call.

That’s how you use AI to give clients something better - not just make the old model more efficient.

If you’re thinking about how AI should reshape legal services, we’d love to hear from you.

evidence.title:
The FTX restructuring ended up costing just under $1 billion. But that's not even the most expensive US restructuring.

Lehman Brothers still holds the record for the most expensive one by reported professional costs: about $2.2 billion by 2013.

Purdue Pharma's final fee approvals in July 2026 put it at about $1.1 billion. Puerto Rico's Title III proceedings were already at about $1.1 billion in June 2023 reporting, and work was still ongoing.

Enron, long treated as the benchmark after Lehman, sits fifth at about $793 million.

These totals cover financial advisers and other professionals as well as lawyers, often working for different sides. 

The full top ten, with dates for each, is in this week's Ledger.

Link in the comments 👇

evidence.title:
9,097 burglar alarm calls. 6 had a break-in in progress or a suspect nearby.

That's Pittsburgh in 2023, from the city's own analysis. Seattle's numbers point the same way: about 13,000 alarm calls in 2023, and under 4% were confirmed to involve a crime. Since October 2024, Seattle police no longer respond to most alarms unless audio, video or a person confirms a crime in progress.

For dealerships, construction sites, equipment yards and storage in cities like these, an alarm on its own isn't enough to get a response. Proof is.

Verdun adds that step. AI agents review every video alarm. Only real threats go to trained operators, who watch live and act: they speak through the site speaker or call police.

evidence.title: Vyra YC Launch - Edit Videos Faster
evidence.text:
Vyra (YC F26) is building the personal video editing agent for shortform content. 

Today, creators, businesses, and founders are spending hours manually editing content. Vyra learns your taste and edits autonomously, vastly speeding up the pace of content creation and enabling anyone to post consistently.

→ Turn messy recordings into viral videos in minutes
Whether it’s talking head footage, launch videos, or hours of random clips - Vyra consolidates your story and makes it social-ready. 

→ Build personalized video libraries
Directly import reference videos from Instagram or TikTok. Vyra will analyze the style and apply it to your own projects + templatize your own video formats so edits are done in minutes. And the agent learns from every project you create.

→ Edit from anywhere
With Vyra’s agents running on the cloud, you can upload your footage, give it your prompt, and close the app. Check back in, and the video will be done :) 

Vyra’s users are already making daily reels for founder-led content, creating 1000s of UGC videos with the MCP, editing personal vlogs, and everything else in between. 

Sulan’s a creator with over 80k+ followers on Instagram, and Caleb’s a video editor of 7 years who previously built plugins for Premiere Pro, Davinci Resolve, and After Effects. As a creator + editor team, they experienced this problem firsthand, and now they’re out to solve it :)

Create now at https://www.usevyra.com!

evidence.title:
The 'vibe-coding' hype obscures a deeper truth.

AI won't replace developers, but it will stratify them into two groups.

On one side, you have the trauma holders. The ones who bel
evidence.text:
The 'vibe-coding' hype obscures a deeper truth.

AI won't replace developers, but it will stratify them into two groups.

On one side, you have the trauma holders. The ones who believe things should be hard because they were hard. They're stuck in 2020 mental models while juniors with AI-powered velocity lap them.

These are good developers. They know their craft. But they can't unlearn the muscle memory that says "this should take 3 days" when AI can scaffold it in 20 minutes.

I was in this camp. Refused to touch Cursor for months because "real developers don't need autocomplete on steroids". Then I watched a junior ship a feature in 2 hours that would've taken me a week the old way.

That's when it clicked. The skill isn't fighting AI. It's embracing parallel workflows.

On the other side, you have the adapters. The ones who treat AI like any other tool in their stack. They're not replacing their skills, they're multiplying them.

They're the ones shipping 3 features while you're still setting up your environment the "right way".

My advice: stop treating AI adoption like a moral choice. It's just another tool. Learn it with the same curiosity you learned Git, Docker, or whatever framework you swear by now.

There are things it crushes and things it can't touch. Figure out which is which.

evidence.title: Aucert (YC F26): AI experts that test your mobile app before it ships
evidence.text:
On mobile, you don't decide when a fix reaches your users — users do. Every release has to be right before it ships.

Aucert is a team of AI experts that test your mobile app on their own. Point them at your build, start a scan, and they use the app like a real person — tapping, typing, screen by screen. Each expert brings a specialty: Pax knows Google Play Store policies inside out, Iris understands accessibility. They learn your product, define what to test, validate your build, and catch what's easy to miss — like a Play Store policy violation that would have blocked the release. You see exactly what broke, with evidence. Your team decides what ships.

Most tools help you write test cases. Aucert's agents do the actual testing.

We've built mobile apps for billions of users. We built Aucert because we wanted it ourselves.

Aucert is part of Y Combinator's F26 batch.

evidence.title:
Kroger cut $120 million of inventory from its pharmacies, and they ran out of stock less often, not more often.

Every pharmacy has to decide, for each drug, when to reorder and how much to keep on the shelf. Kroger makes that decision across 1,950 pharmacies. In 2011, its operations research team and professors from Wright State University built a model that looks at each store's real prescription history and sets those levels for every drug in every store.

What changed:
- $120 million less inventory
- 1.6 million fewer out-of-stock prescriptions a year
- $80 million more in sales a year
- about $10 million a year saved in staff time spent ordering

If your team still sets reorder levels with fixed rules or a spreadsheet, we'd like to hear how you do it.

evidence.title:
Microsoft's cloud runs in more than 400 data centers across more than 70 regions. Every piece of hardware that goes into them needs a supplier, a data center and a delivery date.

Until a few years ago that was planned with manual, spreadsheet-driven processes, and the demand kept growing.

Microsoft's cloud supply chain team and Microsoft Research replaced them with an optimization system. For each request for capacity it chooses the supplier, the data center and the timeline, then fine-tunes the dock dates. In 2023 they added OptiGuide, a language layer on top of the model, so a planner can ask why a decision was made, or what happens if something changes, and get an answer without waiting for an analyst.

What changed, as reported by INFORMS:
- cycle times cut in half
- tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in savings a year
- the average answer to a planner's question went from 2.5 days to near real time

It won the 2026 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: a model that commits to the plan and a layer that explains it to the people who own it, built in weeks on the data an operation already has.

If your team reworks the plan by hand every time demand shifts, we'd like to hear how you do it.

evidence.title:
Chevron runs its seven refineries on one linear program, and puts its value at close to $1 billion a year.

A refinery has to decide which crudes to buy, what to make from them, how to run each unit, and where to invest next. The prices move daily, the chemistry doesn't, and the combinations are endless.

For more than 30 years Chevron has answered those questions with a linear program with distributive recursion, a tool it built and kept improving in-house, now called PETRO. It sits in both day-to-day operations and strategic planning at all seven company-owned refineries.

What it is worth, by Chevron's own estimate:
- value approaching $1 billion a year
- about $10 billion cumulatively over three decades
- one model for feedstock purchases, product slates, unit operation and capital projects

It was a finalist for the 2013 Franz Edelman Award.

Thirty years is what it took a major with its own team. That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a plant with one site and no OR department, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your plant's recipe and purchasing decisions still live in separate spreadsheets, we'd like to hear how they meet.

evidence.title: Pomerado (YC F26) - faster, cheaper, more reliable browser use
evidence.text:
Pomerado turns any website into an API / MCP, in minutes. We are the faster (2-4x), cheaper (10-1000x), and more reliable (+30%) alternative to browser use.

Pomerado works by building a deterministic API on the fly based on a user prompt. It scans the website and translates the task into HTTP calls or Playwright scripts. These APIs are self healing: they detect website changes automatically and repair themselves - no human in the loop required. 

Pomerado works on any website. Use it to supercharge a personal assistant on web tasks. Businesses can integrate agents with ERPs, CRMs, EHR, insurance portals, and more.

Sign up for free at https://pomerado.ai, and check out the open source at https://github.com/Pomerado/pomerado.

evidence.title: Spacesheep makes agent work easy to understand
evidence.text:
Spacesheep is the collaboration surface for people and agents.

Any agent can turn a session's output into a space: a document, a mockup, a live dashboard, slides, or a working app with a backend, like a CRM or a team tool. Share it with one link, and your team works on it together with AI: comment on the exact spot, and an agent makes the change live for everyone.

Several agents can work on the same space, and they use it as shared memory. Every space is indexed for search by meaning, so you and your agents can always find it again.

Teams use Spacesheep for:
- Research
- Design docs and reviewing session output
- Live dashboards
- Slides
- Design mocks
- Internal apps

evidence.title: Deploy (YC F26) - The Generalist Robot Deployment Company
evidence.text:
Deploy puts generalist robots to work in real businesses as a service. You pay for the work getting done, not the robot.

Generalist robot models can finally handle messy, variable work like returns, kitting, and mixed orders. But a capable model isn’t the same as a robot reliably running a shift on your floor. Deploy closes that gap.

How it works:
→ We break each task into steps and track progress in real time
→ The system knows what’s done, what’s next, and when a robot needs help
→ Every human intervention becomes training data, so robots get better the longer they run

Built by Irene and Sahith, robotics engineers from Honda Research Institute and AeroVect. Backed by Y Combinator (F26).

Run a 3PL, warehouse, or distribution center with work that’s hard to staff or automate? Let’s talk.
🌐 deployrobotics.co
✉️ founders@deployrobotics.co

The startup is Skyfall AI, and its AI, called Steve, is a team of agents that answers customers, rewrites listings, cuts ads that don’t sell and changes offers and discounts.

One business, a social media tool, more than doubled from $3,649 a month to $8,307 in about three months. But a Shopify app whose revenue had been falling for five years is still 3% below where it was when they bought it.

And Steve doesn’t get a free hand. It can approve a refund up to $30 on its own, but bigger ones wait for a human to say yes.

That rule matters more than people think. Most teams building AI agents focus on making the AI smarter, but the ones that win will decide exactly what it’s allowed to do without asking.

So within five years, most small online businesses will be run by AI, with one person approving the big decisions. Would you trust an AI to run yours?

evidence.title: “Follow the North Star”
evidence.text:
“Follow the North Star”
30 in. x 18 in.
oil on canvas 
2025

created for my painting class prompt: “obsession”

i’ve been recently obsessed with trying to figure out my “why” - my “north star.” amid college, internships, interviews, and networking there’s a rush, a pressure to have it all figured out. to follow one of the three preset paths: doctor, lawyer, investment banker.

but my heart is not drawn to any of those three paths. it is drawn to creativity, entrepreneurship, design - uncertainty, spontaneity, curiosity. so as i try to figure out what i want to do with my life, i hope that i’ll follow what my heart wants, follow my north star. 

(and the little ghost figures serve as my little homages to all that have supported me! thank you for all your love, i am beyond grateful 🥰)

evidence.title:
UPS expected to save $300 to $400 million a year by changing one thing: the order in which its drivers make their stops.

UPS drivers are known for avoiding left turns, which cuts idling and accidents. The bigger gain came from ORION, an optimization model that plans the stop order for each of its 55,000 US drivers every day, with left turns as one input among many.

Once fully rolled out in 2016, UPS expected it to cut 100 million miles and 10 million gallons of fuel a year. Its drivers already knew their routes well. The model still found that much.

ORION took UPS more than 10 years and about $250M to build, which most companies can't justify.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for routes, production and staffing, built in weeks on the data a company already has. If your team still plans routes in a spreadsheet, we'd like to hear how.

evidence.title:
Taco Bell cut its restaurant payroll by more than $40 million over four years by deciding, 15 minutes at a time, how many people it needed behind the counter.

In a Taco Bell, 52 percent of the day's sales happen in the three hours around lunch, and demand can swing by 1,000 percent inside half an hour. Labor is about 30 cents of every sales dollar. Until 1993 each manager was handed a labor budget as a percentage of sales and left to staff the shifts from experience.

Between 1990 and 1992 the company built three models that work together: a forecast of customer arrivals in 15-minute slots, a simulation that turns arrivals into the staff needed to keep the queue under three minutes, and an integer program that schedules who starts when. Managers review the schedule and change it if they see a reason.

What changed, by Taco Bell's own comparison with the old system:
- $3.5 million saved in 1993, rising to $16.4 million in 1996
- over $40 million in labor cost over those four years, over $53 million through 1997
- about one hour less labor per restaurant per day

It was a finalist for the 1997 Franz Edelman Award.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of staffing model for a warehouse or a plant, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your shift plan is still a percentage of sales and a manager's gut, we'd like to hear how.

evidence.title:
CSX estimates that one system for assigning empty railcars saves it more than $51 million a year, and has spared it $1.4 billion in railcars it never had to buy.

Every day the railroad has to match its empty cars to customer orders. It used to do that one car at a time, with a rule-based system that automated the decision but left cars travelling a long way empty. A weekly optimization run gave a view of the whole network, but its plan went out of date as conditions changed, and cars already assigned could not be reassigned.

In 1997 CSX put in Dynamic Car Planning, by its account the first real-time system of its kind on a US railroad. The published study is by CSX's team and Michael Gorman of the University of Dayton. The system takes in new orders and newly available cars continuously, decides which empty car goes to which order across the network, revises earlier assignments when a better one appears, and sends the changes to the field automatically.

What changed, by CSX's estimate, as reported in 2009:
- more than $51 million a year saved, from less fuel, crew time and car depreciation as empty miles fell
- $561 million saved since 1997
- $1.4 billion in capital spending avoided, because a smaller fleet covers the same business

It was a finalist for the 2009 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a fleet of trailers, containers or rental equipment that has to be in the right place before the order arrives, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team repositions empty equipment one unit at a time, we'd like to hear how you decide.

evidence.title:
In its fiscal year 2023, Walmart took 108,000 truck routes off the road and saved $91.5 million, by its own count. The model behind it plans each route and how the trailer is loaded at the same time.

Walmart's 47 grocery distribution centers in the United States supply more than 4,700 stores and 600 Sam's Clubs. By 2021 the trucks carrying dry groceries were already nearly full by weight and space under the loading system then in use, so there was little left to gain from improving one step on its own.

Walmart's own team built Load Planner. Each day it decides which stores share a truck, in what order they are served, when the driver takes breaks, and where every pallet sits in the trailer, with chilled and frozen goods in their own compartments. It gives itself at most 15 minutes to plan the routes for a distribution center. After a pilot at one center in 2020, it was in use at all 47 by July 2022.

What changed in fiscal 2023, by Walmart's count:
- 108,000 truck routes eliminated, covering 33 million miles
- $91.5 million saved
- 98.6 million pounds of CO2 emissions prevented

It won the 2023 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of routing and loading model for a fleet of 30 trucks, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team plans the routes first and works out the loading afterwards, we'd like to hear how you do it.

evidence.text:
ArchGen Labs (YC F26) is building skyscrapers for semiconductor chips.

AI needs more compute, but shrinking transistors is getting harder and more expensive. Stacking computation vertically can shorten connections and reduce the energy spent moving data.

ArchGen builds the tools to design these 3D chips, helping engineers optimize placement, timing, and temperature together.

Our foundational model for thermal simulation, predicts temperature roughly 5,000× faster than conventional EDA tools and our core placement engine ranked #1 globally in Hudson River Trading’s macro-placement challenge.

We are working with some of the largest fabs in the world to build 3D chips, targeting our first tape out in April 2027.

Building 3D chips or AI accelerators? Reach out to hari@archgen.tech and naveen@archgen.tech

evidence.title: Telamont (YC F26) - AI that catches errors in construction drawings
evidence.text:
Errors are hiding between your construction drawings, specs and contracts. Telamont catches them before they reach the field.

If you build, design or own complex construction projects, book a demo.

Telamont (YC F26) catches the errors hiding between construction drawings, specs and contracts the moment they appear, before they become disputes.

Construction projects lose money in the gap between what the documents say and what gets built. The average construction dispute now runs $60.1 million. The #1 cause? Errors and omissions in those same documents, caught too late.

Telamont connects to where construction documents already live and pulls in every file as it lands, continuously building a complete understanding of the project. Every page is checked against the rest of the project, and risks are flagged immediately.

Instead of reviewing documents, teams act on flagged risks, tracking each from detection to resolution while managing exposure and pursuing recovery opportunities across projects.

Charles grew up in a third-generation construction family and saw firsthand how document errors turn into costly disputes. He was previously a software engineer at 1Password. William was previously a software engineer at Poka, where he applied AI to manufacturing operations. Their team includes people from WSP and AtkinsRéalis, two of the world’s largest engineering firms.

evidence.title: Introducing Composal: A swarm of agents that tests your product like real users
evidence.text:
Coding agents can build a feature, pass every test, and still ship broken flows to your users. Something is broken with how we test today.

Composal is the software factory: a continuous engine that builds, tests, ships, and improves your product.

It deploys a swarm of agents that learn your product by using it. They map its features and explore user journeys in parallel, each with a different role, goal, and approach. When they find a problem, they capture the recording, logs, and steps to reproduce it. That evidence is used to make a fix, then Composal runs again to verify the result.

Every run builds on the last. What the swarm learns becomes product memory and repeatable Scenarios, ready for the next change.

CI checks your code. CD lets you ship continuously. Continual Agent Verification lets you monitor, test, and verify what you're delivering: it checks that your users can still reach their goals as your product evolves.

Verification is our first step toward a self-healing software factory that takes your idea to production and keeps improving it.

You set the direction. Your agents take it from there.

Start your verification journey: composal.com

evidence.title: Posting more actually works🔥
evidence.text:
Posting more actually works🔥

We ran the numbers in our own research, with 50 businesses from January to April 2026.

It shows:
📈 9x more posts published per month
🌐 5x more monthly organic reach
✅ 93% grew their reach
🔥 9 of them went from completely silent to consistently active

So volume wins, but only when the content still sounds like you.

Our data shows that the amount of contextual awareness the AI has about you and the brand, the adoption and engagement of the content itself increases.

In 2025 the word "AI slop" racked up 2.4 million mentions online. 82% of them were negative.

Todays audiences punish AI-made content. But only when the content sounds or looks low-effort. If it looks good, it has the opposite effect.

It can actually help you grow your account and make people feel good about what you are posting.

That's the whole game.

Post more, but only with something that actually sounds like you.

Read more about our research with the link in comments.

evidence.title: Evardi: Agents that engineer the grid edge
evidence.text:
Evardi builds AI agents that engineer the grid edge: the transformers and local lines where rooftop solar, batteries, EVs and data centers connect.

Major outages cost Americans up to $121B in a single year, and nearly all outages start below the substation, where utilities have very little real-time data. Evardi turns the data a utility already collects into a live digital twin of its network, with a virtual meter on every transformer. Our agents use it to spot outages before customers call, test every plan before it happens and check every switching step before it reaches the field.

Work at a utility, or know someone who does? Reach out at diva@evardi.ai or visit evardi.ai

evidence.text:
PEO or broker? It depends on what your business actually needs.

While both can help you offer employee benefits, they work very differently. A PEO becomes a co-employer and bundles HR, payroll, compliance, and benefits into one service. A broker keeps you independent while helping you find and manage the right benefits strategy.

The right choice often comes down to your size, internal resources, and long-term goals.

Swipe through for a side-by-side comparison.

PEO or broker? It depends on what your business actually needs.

The right choice often comes down to your size, internal resources, and long-term goals.

63% of CMOs say they're missing opportunities because they can't make decisions fast enough, per PwC's latest CMO research. Separately, over 70% of marketers report pressure to deliver short-term ROI, but only 29% are consistently executing an AI strategy across the business.

Put those two numbers next to each other and you get the actual problem. It's not that marketing lacks urgency. It's that the systems feeding decisions are slower than the pressure to make them.

That gap is where budget gets questioned. Not because the strategy was wrong, because nobody could prove it fast enough to matter.

evidence.title:
Small business health insurance costs are heading up another 6.7% in 2026, and most companies will sign that increase without asking one question.
What would a different carrier, plan design or funding structure have charged for the same team?

Our 2026 survey of 503 SMB leaders found 39% took a double-digit increase at their last renewal and 64% made a business tradeoff to cover it, most often cutting raises or bonuses. Yet 41% assumed their broker was already finding savings, and only 6% had checked.

One 44 person firm checked. A 22.8% renewal of 718,457 dollars became a 561,543 dollar plan with better coverage.

The article walks through the levers worth testing before the renewal lands: a full market audit, your risk score, funding structure, HRAs and HSAs, contribution strategy, and when a PEO stops being the cheapest answer.

evidence.title:
Alternatives to employer health insurance exist, but most small companies never price one.

77% of small employers that offer coverage are fully insured, usually because that’s what the broker or payroll provider put in front of them. In our survey of 503 SMB leaders, close to half renew every year without weighing a single alternative.

The gap: $5,914 per employee on level-funded or self-funded plans vs. $8,005 fully insured. On a 40-person team, that’s about $84,000 a year.
I broke down all six options, with cost, tax treatment, and who each one fits, in the article below.

evidence.title:
America used to build everything. Cars, radios, steel, the things that shaped the modern world all came off American factory floors.

Somewhere along the way, we stopped. Building got too slow, too expensive and too hard to coordinate. The knowledge that ran our factories lived in people's heads and on paper, and it left when they did.

Organizely is the AI that brings it back. It holds the whole factory in its mind, from the first raw material to the last box out the door. It never forgets and never sleeps, and it gets smarter with every order.

evidence.title:
Hartford Hospital's ER used to plan for the same number of nurses on its slowest night of the week as on its busiest afternoon.

Building each six-week schedule for about 200 nurses also took managers 88 hours of manual work, and they kept reworking it as requests came in.

Researchers at MIT, including Dimitris Bertsimas and Liangyuan Na, worked with the hospital's nursing leaders on software that sets how many nurses each area needs, shift by shift, and then builds each nurse's schedule around their preferences. The hospital has used it since March 2023.

Tested on the hospital's own data, the model showed:
- 85% fewer overtime shifts for nurses
- 8 to 25% better coverage during short-staffed hours
- 5 to 8% lower staffing cost during overstaffed hours
- about $720,000 a year in projected savings

How does your team build its shift schedules today?

evidence.title:
Schneider National, the largest truckload carrier in the United States, avoided a $30 million a year mistake by testing the policy in a model before rolling it out.

The carrier runs over 6,000 long-haul drivers hauling about 13,000 loads a week. Every change to the rules, where to hire drivers, how to get them home, how to handle border crossings, ripples through the whole network. Dispatchers could judge the effect from experience. Nobody could compute it.

Three engineers from Schneider and three from Princeton spent three years building a simulator that makes dispatch decisions the way the best dispatchers do, using approximate dynamic programming to weigh the future cost of each assignment. It matched the company's historical performance closely enough that management trusted it with policy decisions.

What changed, by Schneider's count:
- a planned driver commitment policy would have cost $30 million a year; the model found an alternative with most of the benefit for $6 million
- $5 million a year from putting new driver home bases in the right places
- late deliveries cut by about half after re-examining service commitments, a preliminary result
- $3.8 million saved on border-crossing training by concentrating that work on fewer drivers

It won the 2009 Wagner Prize for excellence in operations research practice.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a fleet of 50 trucks, built in weeks on the data the dispatch desk already has.

When you change a rule in your fleet, how do you know what it will cost before it happens?

evidence.title:
Intel credits one planning capability with $25.4 billion in benefit since 2009: on average $1.9 billion a year in extra revenue and $1.5 billion a year in lower costs.

Each year Intel plans roughly 400 wafer types that become about 4,000 products. They pass through six or more manufacturing stages at more than 200 of its own and outsourced factories in 13 countries, and a single wafer can have hundreds of thousands of possible routes before it ships. Deciding which products to offer and how to make them means choosing among far more plausible plans than anyone could check one by one.

Intel's own teams built two linked pieces. One generates and tests alternative product designs to find the set that best covers what customers need. The other is a large optimization model that plans the supply chain: what to build, where, and from which wafers. Intel says it analyzes many more scenarios in much less time than the tools it replaced, and answers customers faster.

What changed, by Intel's count, as reported in 2020:
- annual revenue up by an average of $1.9 billion
- annual costs down by $1.5 billion
- $25.4 billion in total benefit since 2009
- 2 billion gallons less water used over the ten years of the project

It won the 2020 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same link between what you sell and what your plant can make, for a manufacturer with one site and a few hundred products, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your product list and your production plan are decided in separate meetings, we'd like to hear how you bring them together.

evidence.title:
At Tata Steel, the share of annealed steel strip within 5°C of its target temperature rose from 30% to 50% once an optimization model took over the furnace setpoints, by the team's count. Fuel use per ton of steel fell 8%.

Continuous annealing heats cold-rolled steel strip to a set temperature so that it gets the right mechanical properties. It is hard to control: the furnace responds slowly and with long delays, the flow of steel through it changes often, every change of steel grade brings a new target temperature, and the furnace zones affect each other. This furnace makes automotive-grade steel, and it had been run under manual control for decades.

Tata Steel's team, with consultancy support from the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, built a model of the furnace from plant trials and historical process data. Every minute, it solves an optimization over the next stretch of operation and sends new temperature setpoints to the furnace, moving smoothly through grade changes without breaking operating limits. It has been fully in operation since January 2023.

What changed, by Tata Steel's count:
- strip within ±5°C of target up from 30% to 50%
- 8% less strip outside the ±15°C band, avoiding reprocessing of 13,000 tons a year on one line alone
- 8% lower fuel use per ton of steel
- savings of US$2.5 million and 10,000 tons of CO2 a year, counting lines in operation and those being commissioned

It was a finalist for the 2024 Franz Edelman Award.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of optimization for a single furnace line at a mid-size heat treater, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your operators reset furnace temperatures by hand at every grade change, we'd like to hear how they decide.

evidence.title:
Baosteel replaced manual planning at its Shanghai plant with four optimization systems, and estimates they were worth $76.81 million from 2007 through 2012.

At the time Baosteel was China's largest steel company and the third largest in the world. Its plant had modern equipment, but production and logistics decisions were still made by planners working from rules and experience. By INFORMS's account that meant frequent late orders and high production, inventory and logistics costs.

In 2005 a research team was asked to build planning tools for the plant. Over the next six years it put in four systems, one for each bottleneck the managers had named: how to batch orders for casting and choose the casting width, which slab goes to which order in the slab yard, which coils are annealed together, and how to consolidate and stow finished steel on ships.

What changed, by Baosteel's estimates:
- $76.81 million in cumulative benefit from 2007 through 2012
- about $19.8 million a year expected from then on
- 585,770 fewer tons of carbon dioxide a year, from lower energy use

It was a finalist for the 2013 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of planning model for a mill, a foundry or a processing plant a fraction of that size, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your planners still batch and sequence orders from experience, we'd like to hear how they do it.

evidence.title: ByteAsk (YC F26): Your AI C++ engineer, and a swarm of them
evidence.text:
ByteAsk (YC F26) is building an AI C++ engineer, and a swarm of them.

Trading systems, rockets, cars and chips run on millions of lines of C and C++, and yet AI writes under 5% of the code actually accepted in enterprise codebases.

ByteAsk reads code the way the build does and understands the decades of discussion behind it, from pull requests, Slack messages and Jira tickets. Hundreds of its agents try fixes in parallel on your own machines, run gdb, perf and the tests on each one, and hand back one pull request with the proof attached.

Results
• Multi-SWE-bench C++: 74% of issues resolved, ahead of Claude Code on the same model
• Same model as OpenAI’s Codex CLI, 72 real C++ issues: as many fixes with 63–80% fewer tokens, and cheaper on all 144 runs
• Indexes LLVM’s build in 13.7 minutes on one machine

Free and open source: https://github.com/anirudhakulkarni/byteask
Papers, code and data: https://byteask.ai/research
Book a demo: https://byteask.cal.com/anirudha/30min
Email: founders@byteask.ai
Website: https://byteask.ai

Built by Anirudha Kulkarni (ex-Optiver) and Pratyush Saini (ex-ThirdAI), repeat founders from IIT Delhi.

evidence.title: Grep AI: Self-improving agents for repetitive work that get smarter and cost lest with every run.
evidence.text:
Grep helps companies create, optimize, and deploy AI agents for repetitive back-office work. Rather than treating every task as a fresh problem, our agents learn across runs to improve how they work and reduce execution costs. Our customers include IG.com, Airwallex, Worldpay, and Citizens Bank.


The Problem: Repetitive work shouldn’t require repeated reasoning

Getting an agent to complete a task once is different from running it thousands of times economically.

Hard-coded LLM workflows like LangGraph and n8n are cheaper to run but struggle with exceptions. General-purpose agents like Codex, Cowork and Copilot offer flexibility, but repeatedly figuring out how to do familiar work is expensive and inconsistent.

We’re building Grep AI for this middle ground: work that requires judgment, but follows patterns an agent can learn, and needs to scale economically.

Grep AI: Self-improving agents that use fewer tokens with every run

Grep focuses on specialized agents for recurring workflows, rather than one general-purpose assistant for everything.

Our harness learns the job as it runs, moving repeatable steps from frontier LLM calls to workflows and code. For example, running 100,000 compliance alerts on Claude Code with Opus 5 costs more than $290,000. With our harness, the same workload costs less than $26,000 – over 90% lower.

The world spends roughly $100 billion a year on experimentation in Life-Science. The cost of experiments hinders R&D departments from following new leads, and stops revolutionizing discoveries in less-funded parts of biotechnology like cosmetics, food, and biomaterials.

Halmos reads litterature, fetches models and data from the internet, trains its own models, and simulates the experiments before they are run. In a collaboration, Halmos matched the best performance from a company's wet-lab campaign in an average of 30% fewer evaluations across repeated simulations.

If you run preclinical R&D, process development, assay development, or fermentation/bioprocess optimization, we want to hear from you. Scope an experiment with us at halmoslabs.com or email hi@halmoslabs.com (enterprise inquiries welcome).
